title: A testis-specific E3 ubiquitin ligase complex governs spermiogenesis and male fertility

paper_content.abstract: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) represents an evolutionarily conserved machinery governing proteostasis through spatiotemporal regulation of protein degradation. While spermatogenesis involves multilayered regulatory mechanisms spanning translation to dynamic post-translational modifications (PTMs), the identity of UPS-associated E3 ligases orchestrating germ cell-specific protein turnover remains elusive. Here, we identify a testis-specific E3 ubiquitin ligase complex comprising elongin B/C, Cullin-2 (CUL2), RING-box protein-1 (RBX1), and SOCS box protein ASB9, designated ECSASB9. Genetic ablation of ECSASB9 in mice via ubiquitous Asb9 knockout (KO) or spermatid-specific elongin B/C conditional KO disrupts spermiogenesis and compromises fertility. Mechanistic studies reveal that ECSASB9 engages tubulin beta 4A (TUBB4A) through substrate recognition, catalyzing K48-linked polyubiquitination at lysine 379 (K379) to promote proteasomal degradation. Notably, Tubb4a K379R knock-in (KI) mice phenocopy the spermiogenesis defects observed upon ECSASB9 deficiency. Clinically, we identify three hemizygous missense variants in X-linked ASB9 among Chinese males with idiopathic infertility. Male mice bearing orthologous ASB9 variant exhibit oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OAT) and subfertility, mirroring human phenotypes. Taken together, our findings establish ECSASB9 as an important regulator of spermatogenic proteostasis and provide mechanistic insights into UPS-mediated tissue-specific degradation, while implicating ASB9 variants in male infertility pathogenesis.
paper_content.introduction:
Cellular proteostasis relies on dynamic regulation of protein synthesis and degradation, governed by a conserved enzymatic cascade involving E1 ubiquitin-activating enzymes, E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes, and E3 ubiquitin ligases. This cascade initiates with ATP-dependent activation of ubiquitin (Ub) by E1, forming a thioester bond between Ub’s C-terminus and the E1 catalytic cysteine. Ub is subsequently transferred to an E2 enzyme, generating a reactive E2~Ub intermediate. E3 ligases then orchestrate substrate specificity by recruiting both the E2~Ub complex and target proteins, catalyzing Ub transfer to substrate lysine residues. K48-linked polyubiquitination marks substrates for recognition and proteolysis by the 26S proteasome.

The remarkable diversity of E3 ligases (>600 in humans) reflects their evolutionary adaptation to target a broad array of substrates. E3s are classified into three structural families: RING (really interesting new gene), HECT (homologous to E6AP carboxyl terminus), and RBR (RING-between-RING). RING-type E3s, the largest class, utilize zinc-coordinating RING or U-box domains to bind E2~Ub and facilitate Ub transfer. Among these, cullin-RING ligases (CRLs) represent modular multi-subunit complexes assembled on cullin (CUL) scaffolds, RING-box proteins, adaptors, and substrate receptors. A prototypical CRL subclass is the ECS complex (Elongin B/C–CUL–SOCS-box protein), where SOCS-box proteins serve as substrate receptors by interacting with the Elongin B/C (ELOB/C) adaptor dimer. This adaptor recruits either a CUL2-RBX1 or a CUL5-RBX2 catalytic core, completing assembly of a functional E3 ligase that directs substrate polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.

Notably, >40 SOCS-box proteins have been identified in mammals, conferring tissue-specific functionality to ECS complexes. For instance, SOCS2 modulates growth hormone signaling through dual regulatory roles, while ASB3 suppresses antiviral immunity by targeting mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) for polyubiquitination and degradation. Tissue-restricted ECS variants include ASB15 in skeletal muscle differentiation, and ASB6 in adipocyte insulin signaling via SH2B2 (SH2B adapter protein 2) degradation. These studies collectively demonstrate that ECS complex composition dictates substrate selectivity and functional specialization across tissues. However, the mechanisms governing ECS assembly heterogeneity and its tissue-specific regulatory logic remain unresolved, necessitating systematic exploration of ECS plasticity in vivo.

In somatic cells, ASB9 is predominantly known to assemble into an ECS complex with CUL5, where it targets mitochondrial proteins such as ubiquitous mitochondrial creatine kinase (uMtCK) for degradation, thereby regulating mitochondrial structure and bioenergetics. This establishes a paradigm where ASB9–CUL5 functions in metabolic regulation. However, whether ASB9 can form alternative, tissue-specific complexes with distinct catalytic cores and functions remains an open question. To address this gap and to systematically explore the heterogeneity of ECS complexes in vivo, we performed tissue-specific proteomic profiling of endogenous ECS complexes in mice, which led to the identification of a testis-specific ECS variant, termed ECSASB9, that is important for spermiogenesis and fertility in mice and humans.
paper_content.results:
IP-coupled proteomic profiling identifies ECSASB9
To systematically assess the heterogeneity of the endogenous ECS complex across mammalian tissues, we conducted comprehensive interactome mapping in 11 adult mouse tissues using ELOB as bait. ELOB, together with ELOC, forms a stable adaptor dimer that is central to the assembly of ECS-type E3 ligases. This ELOB/C dimer serves a dual function: it specifically recruits SOCS-box-containing substrate receptors while simultaneously binding to the cullin (CUL2 or CUL5) scaffold, thereby bridging the substrate-recognition module to the catalytic core of the ligase.

Profiling revealed tissue-specific variability in ECS complex composition. ELOB/C and CUL2 demonstrated constitutive presence across all examined tissues. In contrast, SOCS-box proteins displayed stringent spatial restriction, with NEURL2 and ASB10 exclusively detected in heart, while VHL showed intestinal specificity. Of note, testicular heterogeneity was observed, characterized by the co-enrichment of four SOCS-box proteins: ASB1, ASB3, ASB9, and TCEB3. Among these, TCEB3 exhibited broad distribution (detected in 5/11 tissues), whereas ASB1/3/9 showed strictly testis-specific enrichment. Notably, uterus uniquely harbored both CRL2- and CRL5-type ECS complexes, with CUL5 showing uterus-specific enrichment. Collectively, our multi-tissue interactome reveals considerable combinatorial diversity in the ECS complex.

In our previous studies, we found that Asb1 and Asb3 showed abundant expression during the postmeiotic spermatid elongation phase in mice. Notably, whereas Asb3-deficient mice maintained normal fertility and spermatogenesis, ASB1 formed a functional E3 ligase complex with ELOB to orchestrate the ubiquitination of sulfide-quinone oxidoreductase (SQOR), thereby modulating hydrogen sulfide (H2S) metabolic homeostasis during spermiogenesis. This mechanistic insight was corroborated by the phenotype of Asb1-KO which exhibited compromised male fertility characterized by sperm defects and significant testicular H2S depletion. However, little is known about the distribution and function of ASB9 during spermatogenesis. To this end, we first performed a cross-species conservation analysis of ASB9, which showed that it is highly conserved across diverse taxa. Notably, the structural integrity of both Ankyrin (ANK) and SOCS domains was maintained throughout evolution, strongly suggesting an evolutionarily conserved functional role for this protein. RT‒PCR identified Asb9 as testis-enriched in both mice and humans. In addition, immunostaining uncovered strict spatiotemporal distribution of ASB9 during spermatogenesis. While core ECS components ELOB/C, CUL2, and RBX1 exhibited constitutive expression across all spermatogenic steps, ASB9 first appeared at step 8 spermatids. Its signal intensified through steps 9-14, then sharply declined by step 15. Intriguingly, TCEB3, a ubiquitously identified ECS substrate receptor, displayed complementary dynamics: present from pachytene spermatocytes to step 8 spermatids but undetectable in later steps. This reciprocally phased expression pattern suggests a model where timed replacement of TCEB3 by ASB9 reprograms ECS complex substrate specificity during late spermiogenesis.

Immunofluorescence imaging of testicular single-cell suspensions revealed a skirt-like structure of ASB9 signals surrounding the elongating spermatid head, a topography reminiscent of the transient microtubule-based manchette that is crucial for sperm head shaping. Co-immunostaining with the manchette marker α-tubulin showed precise colocalization in elongating spermatids, confirming ASB9’s location in manchette. Subsequently, we performed Co-IP assays using testicular lysates to validate the IP-LC-MS/MS results. Anti-ELOB antibody precipitated the immunoprecipitates comprising ELOB/C, CUL2, RBX1, and ASB9, demonstrating constitutive assembly of an ECS complex we term ECSASB9. Together, these data suggest testis-specific ECSASB9 functions as a manchette-resident ubiquitination machinery which may be required for sperm head morphogenesis.

Impaired spermiogenesis and fertility in Asb9-KO mice
To investigate the functional significance of ECSASB9 in male fertility, we established an X-linked ubiquitous Asb9 knockout (Asb9-KO) mouse model via CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing. Sanger sequencing verified a 13-bp deletion causing frameshift mutation in hemizygous Asb9-KO males, with subsequent Western blot and immunostaining confirming complete ASB9 protein ablation in Asb9-KO testes. Asb9-KO males exhibited marked subfertility accompanied by smaller testis sizes and lower testis weights compared to wild-type (WT) mice. Epididymal sperm analysis revealed that the sperm count, motility and progressive motility were significantly reduced in Asb9-KO mice relative to WT mice. Notably, head morphology defects, including amorphous, microcephalic, or tapered configurations, as well as acrosomal abnormalities, such as irregular shaping, fragmentation or near-complete absence, were increased in Asb9-KO mice, while tail abnormalities remained statistically comparable between the two groups. Ultrastructurally, WT sperm displayed intact acrosomal caps overlying densely condensed nuclei, whereas Asb9-KO sperm exhibited malformed heads with acrosomal defects ranging from irregular and fragmented structures to near-complete absence. In contrast, the flagellar ultrastructure of Asb9-KO sperm appeared normal, exhibiting the typical “9+2” microtubule doublet arrangement characteristic of functional sperm tails. To investigate the basis of the motility defect despite normal flagellar structure, we measured intracellular ATP levels. Sperm from Asb9-KO mice exhibited a significant reduction in ATP content compared to WT controls, indicating a state of bioenergetic deficit. These collective anomalies define a classical oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OAT) phenotype, explaining the observed subfertility in Asb9-KO males.

Histomorphometric assessment of Asb9-KO and WT testes revealed comparable populations of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells between the two groups. However, morphologically compromised spermatids were evident in Asb9-KO tubules. The increased apoptotic signals in the cauda epididymis of Asb9-KO mice suggest that these deformed spermatids may undergo apoptosis. This interpretation is supported by step-resolved morphometric analysis of Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)- and peanut agglutinin (PNA)-stained spermatids, which revealed normal spermatid numbers and head shaping through step 9 in Asb9-KO mice, but a significant reduction in spermatid number and an increase in head and acrosome defects at steps 10–16 of spermiogenesis.

The manchette, a transient microtubular scaffold composed of α/β-tubulin heterodimers, assembles transiently during mouse spermiogenesis (steps 8–14), serving as the principal architect of postmeiotic nuclear shaping. Given ASB9’s manchette-specific localization, we explored whether the deficiency of ASB9 affects manchette structure across spermiogenesis. Immunofluorescence staining and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed intact manchette assembly in Asb9-KO spermatids at steps 8–9, with normally condensing nuclei and properly overlying acrosomes. However, at step 10, the microtubule bundles in Asb9-KO spermatids were thinner than in WT spermatids, which coincided with the onset of nuclear shaping defects and aberrant acrosomal development. In later steps, aberrant elongation and disorganization of the manchette in Asb9-KO spermatids were accompanied by severe malformation of the sperm head and irregular acrosomal structure. Consequently, by late spermiogenesis when the manchette disassembles, Asb9-KO spermatids failed to complete remodeling, resulting in the production of spermatozoa with misshapen heads and malformed acrosomes. All these results indicate ASB9 as an important modulator of manchette dynamics during murine spermiogenesis, with its deficiency causing OAT through microtubule-dependent nuclear shaping defects.

Given that Asb9 mRNA is detectable in several tissues, with notable expression in the kidney, we assessed whether ASB9 deficiency led to broader pathological consequences. Histopathological examination of key organs, including the brain and lung (tissues rich in motile cilia) and the kidney, revealed no overt morphological abnormalities in Asb9-KO adults compared to WT littermates.

ASB9 facilitates the K48-linked ubiquitination of TUBB4A on K379
To identify substrates of the ECSASB9 complex critical for manchette dynamics, we performed IP-LC-MS/MS on endogenous ASB9 complexes isolated from mouse testes. Comparative analysis of two biological replicates identified 97 overlapping proteins, including ASB9, ELOB/C, and tubulin beta 4A (TUBB4A)—a β-tubulin family member. Reciprocal co-IP validated endogenous interactions between ASB9 and both ELOB/C and TUBB4A in testicular lysates. Immunofluorescence confirmed colocalization of ASB9 and TUBB4A in elongating spermatids. Notably, deficiency of ASB9 increased TUBB4A protein abundance without altering its mRNA levels, implicating post-translational regulation. Consistently, TUBB4A immunoprecipitated from Asb9-KO testes exhibited reduced poly-pan and poly-K48 ubiquitination compared to WT testes, as assessed by pan-ubiquitin and K48-specific antibodies. Given the canonical role of K48 chains in proteasomal degradation, these findings suggest TUBB4A as an ECSASB9 substrate undergoing ubiquitin-dependent degradation.

To mechanistically investigate this regulation, we co-expressed Flag-ASB9 and GFP-TUBB4A in HEK-293T cells. The reciprocal interaction was confirmed by co-IP, while ASB9 overexpression dose-dependently reduced endogenous TUBB4A levels. Cycloheximide (CHX) chase assays revealed decreased TUBB4A stability upon ASB9 overexpression. Moreover, we found that MG132, a proteasome inhibitor, could efficiently restore TUBB4A protein levels even under ASB9 overexpression. In vitro ubiquitination assays revealed that testis-derived ASB9 complexes catalyzed TUBB4A polyubiquitination, a process that was also observed in HEK-293T cells. Ubiquitin mutagenesis narrowed chain specificity to K48, as neither K6/K11/K27/K29/K33/K63 variants nor K48R (Lys48 substituted with arginine) supported conjugation.

Mapping ubiquitination sites using our published ubiquitome data of mouse testis, we identified five candidate lysines (K122, K216, K252, K297, K379) on TUBB4A. Site-directed mutagenesis revealed that only K379 mutation abolished ASB9-mediated polyubiquitination. Correspondingly, TUBB4A-K379R exhibited resistance to ASB9-driven destabilization in CHX assays, pinpointing K379 as the key residue for ECSASB9-dependent proteasomal targeting.

TUBB4A mutation phenocopies the spermiogenesis defects of ASB9 deficiency
To investigate the in vivo role of TUBB4A K379 in manchette integrity, we generated Tubb4a K379R knock-in (KI) mice via CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. Genotypic validation by Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) sequencing confirmed successful introduction of the K379R mutation. As anticipated, Tubb4a-KI mice displayed reduced K48-linked and pan-polyubiquitination of TUBB4A, concomitant with increased TUBB4A protein abundance in testes, while mRNA levels remained unaltered. Although Tubb4a-KI mice developed normally, they exhibited subfertility phenotypes. Testicular appearance and weight showed no significant differences between Tubb4a-KI and WT littermates. However, epididymal sperm analyzes revealed decreased sperm count, sperm motility, and progressive motility in Tubb4a-KI mice compared to WT mice. Furthermore, sperm head and acrosome defects were markedly increased in Tubb4a-KI mice, while tail abnormalities remained comparable to those in WT controls.

Histopathological examination revealed shared spermiogenesis defects between Asb9-KO and Tubb4a-KI mice. As shown in Fig. 4l–o, the elongating spermatids in Tubb4a-KI mice exhibited apparent nuclear and acrosomal deformation, coinciding with aberrant elongation of the manchette cytoskeleton. These structural anomalies correlated temporally with disrupted manchette-mediated nuclear shaping, phenocopying the defects observed in Asb9-KO spermatids. Collectively, these findings uncover TUBB4A K379 as a critical residue governing ubiquitination-dependent regulation of microtubule dynamics during murine spermiogenesis.

ELOB/C maintain ECSASB9 complex integrity to ensure spermiogenesis
While ELOB/C are established binding partners of ASB-family proteins, their functional necessity in ECSASB9-mediated substrate recognition remained undefined. To specifically dissect the role of the late-acting ECSASB9 complex without perturbing earlier ECS functions, we designed a spermatid-targeted knockout strategy. Although ELOB/C are expressed in multiple germ cell types, another ECS substrate receptor, TCEB3, operates from pachytene spermatocytes through step 8 spermatids. Ubiquitous or earlier knockout of Elob/c would disrupt the ECS TCEB3 complex and confound interpretation of phenotypes. To isolate the function of ECSASB9 during late spermiogenesis, we generated Tnp2-Cre transgenic mice and Elob/c-floxed mice. The Tnp2-Cre driver restricts Cre recombinase activity to spermatids beginning at step 8, thereby preserving ECS TCEB3 function while enabling selective ablation of ELOB/C in post-step 8 spermatids. Crossing these strains produced spermatid-specific Elob/c conditional knockout mice (Elob/c-cKO). Immunofluorescence staining confirmed efficient depletion of ELOB and ELOC specifically in elongating spermatids of Elob-cKO and Eloc-cKO testes, respectively.

Breeding assays revealed that Elob/c-cKO males were subfertility despite normal mating behaviors. Testis size and weight remained comparable to WT littermates. However, histopathological analysis of Elob/c-cKO epididymal sperm and testes uncovered an OAT phenotype accompanied by sperm head shaping defects and manchette disorganization, phenocopying Asb9-KO and Tubb4a-KI models.

To dissect the molecular basis of these defects, we interrogated ECSASB9 complex integrity in Elob/c-cKO testes. Immunoblot analyzes revealed coordinated reductions in core components: ELOB/C, ASB9, and RBX1. Additionally, TUBB4A protein levels in Elob/c-cKO testes were significantly increased, consistent with loss of ECSASB9-mediated ubiquitination.

Together, these data reveal ELOB/C as key adaptor for ECSASB9 complex stability, with their ablation triggering aberrant TUBB4A accumulation and consequent failure of manchette-mediated nuclear remodeling during spermiogenesis.

Identification of hemizygous ASB9 variants in four infertile men
To explore a possible role for ASB9 in human male fertility, we screened whole-exome sequencing data from a cohort of 1483 individuals with oligoasthenozoospermia. We identified four infertile men with oligoasthenozoospermia harbored hemizygous X-linked ASB9 missense variants. These included c.542C>T (p.A181V) in families F1 and F3, c.275G>A (p.G92E) in F2, and c.479T>C (p.I160T) in F4. All variants were absent or exceedingly rare in public population databases (gnomAD, 1000 Genomes Project). Furthermore, we specifically examined the data from the large-scale studies involving 2875 infertile men with primary spermatogenic failure and found that none of our reported ASB9 variants were present in that cohort. These ASB9 variants were classified as deleterious by computational predictors (SIFT, PolyPhen-2, CADD). Subsequent Sanger sequencing validated these variants in probands. Notably, all mutated residues reside within the evolutionarily conserved ANK domain of ASB9, as demonstrated by cross-species alignment.

Semen analysis of affected individuals showed severe reductions in sperm count, total motility, and progressive motility. Morphological abnormalities were observed via hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and TEM, including amorphous/tapered/small heads and acrosomal defects. These results suggest that ASB9 also plays an important role in sperm head shaping in humans, and that ASB9 variants are associated with human OAT.

Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) using sperm from variant carriers yielded fertilized embryos and blastocysts in all cases. Three of four couples achieved clinical pregnancies, supporting ICSI as an efficient reproductive strategy for men harboring pathogenic ASB9 variants.

To explore the effect of these missense mutations on ASB9 expression, HEK-293T cells were transfected with Flag-tagged ASB9-WT or mutant constructs (p.A181V, p.G92E, and p.I160T). Western blotting revealed markedly reduced ASB9-G92E protein levels compared to WT, concomitant with TUBB4A accumulation. CHX chase assays revealed rapid degradation of ASB9-G92E, which was rescued by MG132-mediated proteasome inhibition. Ubiquitination assays confirmed enhanced polyubiquitination of ASB9-G92E, indicating that p.G92E destabilizes ASB9 via UPS. Notably, despite ASB9-I160T and ASB9-A181V protein levels being comparable to WT, co-IP assays revealed a marked reduction in TUBB4A binding efficiency. This diminished interaction correlated with reduced TUBB4A polyubiquitination and consequent protein accumulation, identifying I160 and A181 as key residues for ASB9-TUBB4A interactions.

Mice bearing orthologous ASB9 variant mirror human phenotypes
Given the important role of Asb9 in murine spermatogenesis was unveiled by KO studies, we further generated CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Asb9G88E (Asb9-KI) mice (orthologous to human ASB9G92E) to validate its functional significance. PCR sequencing confirmed precise targeting of the variant. Similar to our in vitro findings, Asb9-KI testes exhibited increased K48-linked and pan-polyubiquitination of ASB9 alongside markedly reduced ASB9 protein levels, despite unchanged mRNA abundance. Conversely, TUBB4A ubiquitination was diminished in Asb9-KI mice, resulting in elevated TUBB4A protein accumulation without transcriptional alteration.

Notably, while Asb9-KI males exhibited normal mating behavior and testis size, they displayed significant subfertility. Histopathological analysis of Asb9-KI mice revealed OAT phenotypes, characterized by nuclear shaping defects and disorganized manchette structures. Additionally, ICSI using sperm from Asb9-KI males resulted in normal fertilization and development to the 2-cell stage at a rate comparable to the WT control, recapitulating the successful fertilization outcome observed in human carriers. These data conclusively establish the pathogenic cascade initiated by the ASB9G92E variant across species.
paper_content.methods:
Study participants
In this study, a cohort of 1483 men with idiopathic infertility and oligoasthenozoospermia was recruited from the Reproductive Genetic Hospital of CITIC-Xiangya and the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University in China. The recruitment of participants was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the World Health Organization (WHO, 2010). A clinical investigation revealed that all affected individuals exhibited normal development of male external genitalia. The study also excluded other potential causes of infertility, including reproductive malformations, exposure to drugs, and gonadotoxic factors. Meanwhile, all individuals had a normal 46,XY karyotype and no Y-chromosome AZF microdeletion. This study was conducted in strict accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethical Committee of Reproductive Genetic Hospital of CITIC-Xiangya (Approval: LL-CC-2019-034) and the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University (Approval: PJ2020-13-10). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Whole exome sequencing (WES), bioinformatic analysis, and Sanger sequencing
Blood samples were collected from participating individuals, and genomic DNA was extracted using a DNA extraction kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The exome capture was performed using the Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon V6 Kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), and the sequencing was carried out on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). Then, the raw sequencing data were aligned to the human genome reference assembly (GRCh37/hg19) using Burrows–Wheeler Aligner software. PCR duplicates were removed, and the quality of variants was evaluated using the Picard software. Functional variants, including single-nucleotide variants and small insertions or deletions, were annotated using ANNOVAR software.

Candidate pathogenic variants were screened using the following criteria: bi-allelic or hemizygous variants, variants with a minor allele frequency below 5% in the public databases, such as the gnomAD database and the 1000 Genomes Project; variants predicted to be deleterious using multiple tools, including Polyphen-2 (genetics.bwh.harvard.edu/pph2), Mutation Taster (www.mutationtaster.org/), SIFT (sift.jcvi.org/) and Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (cadd.gs.washington.edu/). Subsequently, the candidate variants were further validated through Sanger sequencing in the affected individuals, with the primers listed in Table S4.

Animal models
Asb9, Tubb4a, and Elob/c mutant lines were generated via pronuclear co-injection of Cas9 mRNA and target-specific sgRNAs (Table S5) into C57BL/6J zygotes, followed by oviduct transfer to pseudopregnant females. Founders were backcrossed for five generations with WT C57BL/6J mice to minimize off-target effects.

The Tnp2-Cre line was established using the PiggyBac transposon system. A donor plasmid containing the Tnp2 promoter (−549/−48 bp relative to TSS), Cre recombinase cDNA, and polyA signal was co-injected with transposase mRNA into zygotes prior to embryo transfer. Tnp2-Cre mice were crossed with ROSA26-mT/mG dual-fluorescent reporter mice (Jackson Laboratory, stock no. 007676). Cre-mediated recombination triggered membrane-localized GFP (mG) expression, enabling spatial tracking of recombinase activity.

All genotypes were validated by PCR (primers in Table S4). For fertility assessment, adult males (8 weeks) were individually co-housed with two WT females under standard conditions for 2 months; litter sizes were recorded for statistical analysis.

All male C57BL/6J mice used in this study were 8–12 weeks old. The exact number of animals per experimental group is clearly indicated in the corresponding figure legends. Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free conditions in individually ventilated cages (maximally 5 per cage) with a 12-h light/dark cycle, ambient temperature of 22–26°C, and relative humidity of 50–70%. Sterile food and Mice water were provided ad libitum. Animal health and welfare were monitored daily by trained animal facility staff and the research team; no unexpected mortality or morbidity occurred during the study. At experimental endpoints, mice were euthanized by carbon dioxide inhalation followed by cervical dislocation, and all efforts were made to minimize suffering. All experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Ethical and Welfare Committee of Nanjing Medical University (IACUC licenses: 2004020 and 2402015) and performed in strict accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.

Cell culture and transfection
HEK-293T cells (American Type Culture Collection; ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) were maintained in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, Grand Island, NY, USA) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco) at 37°C/5% CO2. Expression constructs were generated by cloning the following cDNAs into specified vectors: Flag-tagged ASB9 (WT/mutant) into the pcDNA3.1 vector, HA-tagged Ub (WT/mutant) into the pRK5 vector, and GFP-tagged TUBB4A (WT/mutant) into the pEGFP-N1 vector. Transfections were performed using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) per manufacturer’s protocol. Cells were harvested 48 h post transfection for analysis. Plasmid concentrations were standardized at 0.5 μg/mL unless otherwise indicated in figures. All expression constructs used in this study are detailed in Table S6.

RNA extraction, RT‒PCR, and real-time q‒PCR
Total RNA was isolated from tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen), with subsequent cDNA synthesis performed via reverse transcription using HiScript III RT SuperMix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). Commercial human multi-tissue cDNA was purchased from TaKaRa (Shiga, Japan). Gene-specific primers (Table S4) were employed for both RT-PCR (amplification products resolved on 1.5% ethidium bromide-stained agarose gels to confirm amplicon size) and quantitative real-time PCR using SYBR Green chemistry (AceQ MasterMix, Vazyme) on a StepOne System (Applied Biosystems, Waltham, MA, USA). Gene expression levels were calculated by the 2^(−ΔΔCt) method, normalized to 18S rRNA as the internal control.

Western blotting
Protein lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) containing 1% protease inhibitor cocktail (Selleck, Houston, TX, USA), incubated 30 min on ice, and centrifuged (12,000 × g, 50 min, 4°C). Protein concentration was determined by BCA assay (Beyotime). Samples were separated by Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred to PVDF membranes (0.45 μm, Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA). Membranes were blocked in 5% non-fat milk/tris-buffered saline Tween-20 (TBST) for 2 h followed by primary antibody incubation (overnight, 4°C; antibodies in Table S7). After TBST washes, HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies were applied (2 h; room temperature, RT). Protein signals were detected using SuperSignal West Femto Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) on a Tanon 5200 imaging system.

Sperm analysis
Spermatozoa were collected from adult mouse cauda epididymides by mincing in 200 μL modified human tubal fluid (HTF) medium (FUJIFILM Irvine Scientific, Santa Ana, CA, USA) supplemented with 10% FBS (37°C, 10 min). Concentration was quantified via hemocytometer, while motility parameters (total and progressive) were assessed using a Ceros II analyzer (Hamilton Thorne, Beverly, MA, USA), assessing >200 sperm per sample. For morphology analysis, sperm smears were prepared and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 15 min. After PBS washes, the smears were stained with Hematoxylin (Solarbio, Wuhan, China) for 8 min, followed by bluing in running water and counterstaining of the cytoplasm with Eosin Y (Solarbio) for 2 min. Finally, the slides were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, cleared in xylene, and mounted with neutral balsam for morphological examination under a microscope (Axioskop 2 Plus, Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany).

ATP measurement
Caudal epididymal sperm were lysed using the ATP Assay Kit (Beyotime) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Following a 15-min centrifugation at 12,000 × g and 4°C, the supernatant was collected for analysis. A standard curve was generated using serial dilutions of ATP stock solution in the provided lysis buffer, yielding final concentrations of 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, and 10 μM. The working reagent was equilibrated at room temperature for 3 min prior to use. Supernatants were then mixed with the working reagent, and chemiluminescence was measured using a modular multimode microplate reader (BioTek, Winooski, VT, USA). Total protein concentration in each sample was determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Beyotime). ATP levels were normalized to protein content and expressed as nmol/mg protein.

Histological analysis
Testes, brains, lungs, and kidneys were dissected and immediately fixed in modified Davidson’s fluid for a minimum of 48 h at room temperature. The fixed tissues were then processed through a graded ethanol series (70%, 80%, 95%, and 100%) for dehydration, cleared in xylene, and infiltrated with and embedded in paraffin. For histological evaluation, sections of all tissues (5 μm) were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through a graded ethanol series to distilled water. Testicular sections were subjected to PAS staining, while sections of brain, lung, and kidney were stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin. After dehydration through graded ethanols, clearing in xylene, and mounting with neutral balsam (Solarbio), testicular sections were imaged using a bright-field microscope (Axioskop 2 Plus, Zeiss), while brain, lung, and kidney sections were examined using a DS-Ri2 microscope (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan).

For TEM, tissues and sperm were fixed in 2% glutaraldehyde overnight at 4°C. The samples were then post-fixed with 1% osmium tetroxide (OsO4) for 2 h at room temperature. Following fixation, the samples were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series and infiltrated with a mixture of propylene oxide and Araldite 502 epoxy resin before being embedded in pure resin. Ultrathin sections (80 nm) were cut using an ultramicrotome (UC7, Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany), collected on copper grids, and counterstained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate. The grids were examined using a JEM-1410 transmission electron microscope (JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) operated at 80 kV.

For SEM, the sperm samples were processed following the similar fixation and dehydration procedures as described for TEM. The dehydrated samples were then dried using a Critical Point Dryer (K850, Quorum, Laughton, UK), sputter-coated with gold, and observed under a scanning electron microscope (JEOL JSM-7900F).

Immunofluorescence analysis
For tissue sections, paraffin-embedded testicular and lung sections (5 μm) were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through a graded ethanol series to distilled water. Antigen retrieval was performed by incubating the sections in pre-heated 10 mM sodium citrate buffer (pH 6.0) and heating in a microwave oven for 15 min. After washing three times with PBS (pH 7.4), sections were blocked with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA; Solarbio) for 2 h at room temperature. Subsequently, sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies (Table S7). After PBS washes, Alexa Fluor-conjugated secondaries were applied for 2 h at room temperature in the dark. After three additional PBS washes, nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (5 μg/mL; Beyotime). Finally, the slides were washed with PBS and mounted with anti-fade fluorescent mounting medium (Beyotime). Images were acquired using an LSM800 confocal microscope (Zeiss). For single-cell suspensions, testes were enzymatically digested with collagenase IV (1 mg/mL, Invitrogen) for 15 min at 37°C and trypsin (0.25%, Gibco) for 10 min at 37°C, respectively. Reactions were quenched with DMEM/10% FBS. The cell suspension was passed through a 40-μm cell strainer to remove aggregates, and the cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 800 × g for 5 min. Pelleted cells were resuspended, fixed on slides using 4% PFA, and washed three times with PBS. Subsequently, samples were blocked with 1% BSA (Solarbio) for 2 h at room temperature. Immunostaining was then performed following the similar procedure as described for tissue sections.

For sperm, sperm smears were prepared and fixed with 4% PFA for 15 min at room temperature. After PBS washes, samples were blocked with 1% BSA (Solarbio) for 2 h at room temperature. Subsequent immunofluorescence staining steps were performed identically to those described for tissue sections.

Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL)
Apoptosis was detected using a commercial kit (Vazyme) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, deparaffinized cauda epididymis sections were rehydrated, permeabilized with proteinase K (10 μg/mL) for 10 min at room temperature. After washing three times with PBS, the sections were incubated with Equilibration Buffer for 30 min at room temperature and incubated with Bright Red reagent at 37°C for 60 min. After PBS washes, nuclei were counterstained with DAPI prior to confocal imaging (LSM800, Zeiss).

IP-LC‒MS/MS analysis
Tissues from 8-week-old mice were homogenized on ice in RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime) containing 1% protease inhibitor cocktail (Selleck). The homogenates were incubated on ice for 30 min and then centrifuged at 16,000 × g for 30 min at 4°C to remove insoluble debris. Lysates were pre-cleared with 20 μL of Dynabeads™ Protein A (Invitrogen) for 3 h at 4°C. The pre-cleared lysates were then incubated overnight at 4°C with gentle rotation with the specified antibody (Table S7). The following day, 40 μL of Dynabeads™ Protein A was added to the lysate-antibody mixture and incubated for an additional 3 h at 4°C with rotation. Precipitates were washed (3 × RIPA buffer), boiled in 2 × SDS buffer (5 min), and resolved by SDS-PAGE. Gel bands were excised (≈1 mm³), destained (H2O→50% ACN→100% ACN), reduced (56°C, 1 h), alkylated (45 min, RT, dark), and digested with trypsin (37°C, 12 h). Peptides were acidified (0.1% TFA), extracted, SpeedVac-dried, desalted via StageTip, and analyzed by LTQ Orbitrap Velos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Raw files were processed in MaxQuant (v1.3.0.5) against the UniProt mouse database with tryptic specificity (≤2 missed cleavages), 1% FDR thresholds, fixed carbamidomethylation (+57.0215 Da), and variable modifications (methionine oxidation, N-terminal acetylation). Label-free quantification ratios were computed, with >10-fold changes defining candidate interactors.

Co-IP assay
For exogenous co-IP, transfected HEK-293T cells were lysed on ice for 30 min in RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with 1% protease inhibitor cocktail. The lysates were centrifuged at 16,000 × g for 15 min at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected. A small aliquot (10%) of the supernatant was saved as the “Input” control. The remaining lysates were incubated overnight at 4°C with anti-Flag magnetic beads (Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA) or anti-GFP magnetic beads (Proteintech, Rosemont, IL, USA). For endogenous co-IP, testicular lysates underwent primary antibody incubation (overnight, 4°C) followed by 3-h capture with Dynabeads™ Protein A (Invitrogen) at 4°C. In both methodologies, bead-bound complexes were collected using a magnetic rack and subsequently washed with lysis buffer (Beyotime). After the final wash, the bound proteins were eluted by boiling the beads in 2 × SDS buffer at 95°C for 10 min. Both the Input controls and the Co-IP eluates were then subjected to immunoblotting with target-specific antibodies (Table S7).

Cycloheximide chase analysis
Protein stability was assessed using a cycloheximide (CHX) chase assay. In short, HEK-293T cells in 6-well plates were transfected for 48 h. To inhibit new protein synthesis, the cell culture medium was replaced with fresh medium containing 100 μg/mL CHX (Sigma). Cells were then harvested at specific time points post-CHX treatment. Protein degradation kinetics were assessed by immunoblotting.

In vitro ubiquitination assay
ASB9 immunoprecipitates were isolated from mouse testicular lysates via immunoprecipitation and then incubated in reaction buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 5 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 2 mM ATP) containing 100 nM E1, 2 μM UbcH5a (E2), 2.5 μM Ub, and 10 μg His-TUBB4A (Sangon, Shanghai, China). The reaction was incubated at 37°C for 2 h with gentle shaking. Reactions were terminated with SDS buffer (95°C, 10 min) and immunoblotted.

In vivo ubiquitination assay
Tissues or transfected HEK-293T cells were lysed in SDS-denaturing buffer (1% SDS, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl). The samples were immediately boiled for 10 min to denature proteins and inactivate cellular enzymes. The lysates were then cooled on ice and diluted tenfold with NP-40 lysis buffer. The diluted lysates were centrifuged at 16,000 × g for 15 min at 4°C, and the supernatants were subjected to immunoprecipitation overnight at 4°C with the appropriate antibody (Table S7). Complexes were resolved by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotted.

ICSI for mice
The sperm from the cauda epididymides of adult WT and Asb9-KO mice was retrieved and added into the HTF medium. For ICSI, cumulus intact oocytes were collected from the oviduct of superovulated 4-week-old C57BL/6J female mice. Subsequently, hyaluronidase from bovine testes (Sigma, H4272) was used to remove the cumulus cells. The sperm head was injected into an oocyte. Then, the injected oocytes were cultured in KSOM medium (Millipore) in 6% CO2 at 37°C. The 2-cell embryo was counted 20 h later.

ICSI for ASB9 mutation-associated infertile men
Four females, whose partner harboring hemizygous ASB9 missense mutations, consented to ICSI treatment. They underwent controlled ovarian hyperstimulation, oocyte retrieval, ICSI, and had pregnancy confirmed. Pregnancy confirmation was achieved through two hCG tests conducted 14 days after embryo transfer. A clinical pregnancy was defined as the visualization of at least a gestational sac with a fetal heartbeat via ultrasound screening 28 days post embryo transfer.

Statistics and reproducibility
Data represent mean ± SD. All experiments were performed at least three independent replicates. Analyzes used GraphPad Prism 8.0: two-tailed unpaired t-tests (two groups) or one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) with Dunnett’s test (multiple groups). Significance was defined as p < 0.05. Biological replicates are specified in figure legends. All schematic diagrams and cartoons presented in this study were originally created by our team using Adobe Illustrator (version 2021).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study comprehensively reveals the anti-MRSA mechanisms of Candesartan Cilexetil from multiple dimensions. The writing style is professional and standardized, adhering to the requirements of academic papers. The figures are clear and intuitive, with precise English labeling of specialized terms. The references are comprehensive and up-to-date, reflecting the latest research progress in this field. The work exhibits somewhat time-sensitive, and its technical route is complete with prominent innovation. However, the depth of mechanism analysis (e.g., the association between dynamic membrane behavior and metabolic regulation) requires further enhancement, and the rigor of experimental design needs improvement. With revisions, this work is expected to become a landmark study in the field of membrane-targeted antibiotic research.
The following suggestions and comments are put forward:
1. Clearly distinguish between "main findings" and "mechanism interpretation." For example, explicitly state "CC reduces C20:0 fatty acid levels to impair membrane fluidity" as a standalone mechanism rather than implying it within result descriptions.
2. Supplement the direct correlation between the membrane structure of MRSA and its drug resistance. In particular, the impact of membrane lipid composition (such as phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin) on drug penetration should be emphasized to strengthen the logicality of the research background.
3. Elaborate on the contrast between "CC-induced membrane rigidity" and "traditional membrane-active agents increasing fluidity" , and put forward a reasonable explanation based on the membrane lipid phase transition theory.
4. Discuss potential compensatory mechanisms for the absence of C20:0 synthesis-related genes in resistant mutants.For example, the substitution of other fatty acids or adaptive changes in membrane proteins.
5. Emphasize integrated analysis of multi-omics data. For example, instead of merely listing data,explore the correlation between the down-regulatation of cell wall synthesis genes in the transcriptome and the reduction of phospholipids in the lipidome.
6. Validation of membrane disruption mechanisms:
a.Molecular Dynamics Simulation: It is recommended to add simulations with different membrane lipid ratios (such as DOPC/DOPG/CL mixed membranes) to better approximate the real MRSA membrane environment.
b. Metabolomics and Lipidomics Analysis: It is necessary to verify whether the down-regulation of key metabolites, such as UDP-N- acetylglucosamine, directly leads to cell wall synthesis defects. It is also advisable to analyze the changes in membrane lipid asymmetry after CC treatment to establish a connection with the increase in membrane permeability.
c. Functional Verification of Mutant Strains: Gene knockout or complementation experiments are required to confirm the contribution of mutant genes (e.g., tarS) to CC resistance, excluding the interference of other SNPs.
7.Structure-Activity Relationship Research: The scope of toxicity testing on mammalian cell lines needs to be expanded to evaluate the potential mammalian toxicity of CC.
8. Optimization of In Vivo Models: It is necessary to supplement the monitoring of the local concentration of CC at the infection site, improve its pharmacokinetic data, and clarify its tissue distribution characteristics.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
There is a need to develop new therapeutic approaches to combat drug-resistant pathogens such as MRSA. Given the technical and economic challenges associated with antibiotic development, there is justifiable interest in re-purposing FDA-approved drugs as antibacterials. As such, there is a sound rationale for the work described in the manuscript.
The authors have clearly done a lot of work, but unfortunately the very large volume of data/number of panels in graphs makes the manuscript hard to follow, particularly since there simply isn’t enough explanation of why certain conditions were chosen, how one experiment led to the next and what the advances are. For example, synergy was reported for gentamicin and polymyxin B, which aren’t the first antibiotics one thinks of for treating MRSA – were others tried? Are these the only ones that showed synergy and are the authors proposing to use polymyxin B to treat MRSA infections?
I also have concerns about the novelty of the work since reference 21 reported that CC has anti-staphylococcal bactericidal activity, anti-biofilm activity, is antibacterial in vivo, measured host cell cytotoxicity, synergized with gentamicin and caused membrane damage, it’s not clear how much of this work is novel. The authors acknowledge this previous work and provide some additional mechanism, but I’m not convinced that it’s a significant advance.
Additional major points
1. The results are difficult to interpret as there is a lack of consistency in concentrations used throughout the different assays and in some cases, inoculum sizes.
2. There is a lack of suitable statistics and descriptions of statistics used throughout the paper. The authors also make comparisons between panels, e.g., Line 218: ‘Comparison of Fig. 4A with Fig. 4B’, without performing statistics between these comparisons. I would suggest, when doing this, to show fewer concentrations and combine the panels into one panel. Two-way ANOVA should be performed on time-kill assays.
3. Fluorescence-based assays, e.g., Sytox and DiSC3(5), should be OD600nm corrected to account for any changes to the bacterial inoculum density.
4. I am not sure that the DiSC3(5) assay has been performed correctly. When the membrane potential is intact, this voltage-sensitive dye is self-quenched, as the authors show. Compounds capable of depolarizing the membrane cause the dye to leak out, causing an increase in fluorescence. CCCP is also incompatible with this assay due to its interference with the fluorescence of DiSC3(5). Valinomycin or gramicidin would be a more suitable control, see 10.3389/fcell.2016.00029
5. I would suggest to the authors to reduce some of the modelling and SAR to improve the clarity of the message. This would make for a nice follow up paper.
6. It’s not clear why Polymyxin was assayed here, since it’s not used to treat infections caused by S. aureus. Some rationale for this should be provided. Daptomycin would be a much more appropriate choice.
7. Since CC is only active against S. aureus in the pro-drug form, which is converted in gastric epithelial cells, how viable is this as a therapeutic? Are the MIC concentrations reported here achievable in vivo?
Minor points
Line 38: I don’t understand why ‘The severity of S. aureus infections is reflected in the wide variety of S. aureus virulence factors’. Some pathogens cause disease via a single toxin. I would understand if range of virulence factors was linked to range of different types of disease but not severity.
Line39: persistence and tolerance don’t enable resistance. The former confer survival, and the latter the ability to grow, in the presence of antibiotics.
Line 52: Omit ‘lipopolysaccharides’, as S. aureus does not have LPS and LPS is not a negatively charged phospholipid.
Line 75: Authors describe a ‘6-log10-CFU/ml’ reduction to the limit of detection. Figure 1B shows a decrease in viability from 107 – 102 CFU/ml, giving a 5-log reduction.
Line 79: A ~30% reduction in biofilm production, I do not believe, constitutes inhibition of biofilm production. Similarly, I do not think you can categorise CC as having biofilm eradication activity. I would recommend using tetracycline or chloramphenicol as a control for biofilm inhibition
Line 102: Can the authors comment on why the all-atom MD simulations performed at Vanderbilt are not in agreement with the prior simulations in reference to membrane perturbation?
Line 93-102: Is CC able to interact with positively charged alterations (lysyl-PG) to the membrane?
Figure 1: Different starting inocula are used between 1B and 1C. 1I and 1J are lacking labels, scale bars, and quantification. 1K and 1L are lacking scale bars and quantification. Lack of stats for 1B, 1C, 1D, 1E, 1F, 1G. ‘Persisters’ should be labeled as ‘stationary phase’.
Line 105: A concentration of 10x MIC is used for AFM studies. Can the authors provide a justification for such a high concentration? Is this concentration clinically achievable?
Line 120: A sub-lethal concentration of CC is used. The authors note in line 116 that they aimed to identify the MOA by which CC kills and identify potential targets, therefore this should be repeated with a lethal concentration of CC.
Line 126: how do the authors explain down-regulation of genes associated with membrane stress during exposure to CC, which damages the membrane?
Figure 2. The colour scheme in 2A is very difficult for the reader to follow.
Line 139-141: Names of metabolites do not need to be capitalised.
Line 147-149: Based on the author's findings that CC causes a decrease in the abundance of key membrane lipids and its synergy with polymyxin B, CC may also synergise with daptomycin.
Line 168-179: Transcriptomic analysis indicates a disruption in peptidoglycan synthesis and production of β-lactam resistance determinants, yet synergy with cell-wall acting antibiotics was not investigated.
Line 170: Please include clarification on how many times the checkerboard analysis was repeated. Is the FICI described the mean/median of multiple replicates?
Line 173: Please see the above comment on high concentrations and persisters.
Line 181-184: Is ATP synthesis affected by CC+gentamicin combination?
Figure 3. A different starting inoculum is used for 3B exponential cells and persisters. Please perform two-way ANOVA analysis on 3B. The labels are cut off on 3D and 3F. Could the authors provide a quantitative measurement of surface disruption/damage in 3E. Concentrations of CC, gentamicin and polymyxin B are not described in the figure legend. How many antibiotics were examined for synergy? Presumably many were tested and only those that showed synergy are shown? 3 of 4 are aminoglycosides, so perhaps not surprising they have similar effects?
Line 218-219: The Authors make a direct comparison between panels without having performed statistics. Please see comment above on comparisons between graphs.
Line 223-225: Please see the above comment on comparisons.
Line 225: Fig. 4N and 4O are referenced before 4F, 4G, 4I, 4J, DK, 4L. Could the authors please re-order Fig. 4 to reflect the text?
Line 230-239: What is the purpose of Fig. 4M? It is not referenced in the text.
Line 240: Could the relative abundance of C20:0 be calculated?
Figure 4. Description of statistics for 4A, 4B, 4C. Stats need to be performed for 4D, 4E. Fluorescence microscopy in 4F-J is too small. Combining panels 4K-L , 4M-O, 4Q-S, 4T-V, 4W-X would give more space for larger microscopy images.
Line 253: A p-value is provided, but there is no description of what statistics were performed.
Line 258: A p-value is provided, but there is no description of what statistics were performed.
Line 267: Needs reference for how pH impacts antibiotic activity.
Line 271: Could the authors comment on the improved potency at low pH despite not having membrane permeabilisation activity.
Line 281: A graph should be included of the serial passaging experiment.
Line 293- Line 295: The authors should investigate the individual involvement of these genes in CC resistance using mutants.
Line 295- Line 300: A see-saw effect is also seen between daptomycin and β-lactams, whereby DAPR is associated with increased susceptibility to β-lactams. Synergy between CC and daptomycin or β-lactams should be investigated.
Line 305-306: Drug names do not need to be capitalised.
Line 359: Does the removal of the ester linker in compound 7 make it less susceptible to esterase activity in the host?
Figure 5. Please see above comments on stats and combining panels where comparisons are made.
Figure 6. Please see above comments on stats
Line 384: What is the difference between membrane perturbation and disruption?
Line 388-389: These abbreviations have already been introduced to the reader.
Line 417: If the ester linker is essential for antibacterial activity, then the authors should consider providing information on the compound's stability in host contexts.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This study found the effectiveness of candesartan cilexetil as an antibiotic against MRSA. In particular, the authors propose that the change in C20:0 fatty acids is associated with the susceptibility of bacteria to CC. While the manuscript presents intriguing data on the potential application of CC as an antibiotic using a variety of experimental approaches, it appears to lack sufficient elucidation of the underlying mechanism and its practical applicability. Moreover, the absence of detailed descriptions for the multi-omics methodology, the low quality of several figures (e.g., small text, missing scale bars), and inaccurate figure legends collectively reduce the overall clarity and credibility of the manuscript.
Major concerns
- The authors should conduct more reliable experiments to identify the potential specific lipid target of CC. The authors should determine the mechanism by which CC treatment reduces the production of C20:0 fatty acids. Additionally, they should analyze whether the susceptibility of MRSA to CC changes when genes involved in the relevant biosynthetic pathway are knocked out or overexpressed.
- The precise target lipid associated with the antibacterial activity of CC should be identified (e.g., C20:0-containing phosphatidylcholine).
- While previous studies have correlated increased membrane fluidity with enhanced antibiotic effects as discussed, this study suggests that increased membrane rigidity induced by C20:0 treatment is associated with the antibacterial effect of CC. Further mechanistic studies are needed to clarify this discrepancy.
- The interpretation of the results regarding C20:0-lipid in this manuscript is difficult for readers to follow. For example, Figures 4Q–Y suggest that the treatment of C20:0 fatty acids enhance MRSA susceptibility to CC. However, Fig 4P shows that treatment with CC, which has antibacterial activity, actually decreases C20:0 lipid levels. This apparent contradiction raises questions about whether C20:0 lipids are indeed the potential target of CC. The authors need to provide a clearer explanation of these findings in the manuscript.
- CC is known to have side effects such as low blood pressure, elevated potassium levels, and kidney damage. Using the effective dosage shown in Figure 6, these parameters should be measured. In the case of Fig 6B, the lack of statistical significance may be due to the small sample size (low n), yet it shows a trend of increase potentially induced by CC. These measurements should be analyzed with a higher n and not only at the terminal time point, but also across multiple time points.
- The methods section does not provide details on how the metabolomics and lipidomics analyses shown in Figure 2 were performed.
Minor concerns
- In Fig 1L, clearly label which treatment group each image corresponds to.
- It would be preferable to include scale bars in all microscopy images. (e.g. Fig 1K)
- In Figure 2, downregulation and upregulation are indicated in red and blue in the pathway graph (Fig. 2A), whereas in the heatmaps (Fig. 2B–D), the colors are reversed, downregulation is shown in blue and upregulation in red. This inconsistency within a single figure may cause confusion in data interpretation, so it would be preferable to standardize the color scheme.
- In line 132, Extended Data Fig 2E-right shows individual metabolite levels rather than enriched pathways. Additionally, Extended Data Fig 2E-left does not appear to be a volcano plot. There are also other instances in Extended Figure 2 where the figure panels are incorrectly referenced in the main text. Please review and correct the panel labels accordingly.
- The legend for Figure 4 is incorrectly labeled as Figure 5.
- The description of the panel in Figure 4P should be clarified. The figure legend states that vancomycin was used as a control, but it is not indicated in the panel itself, which leads to confusion in interpretation.
- In line 254, please verify whether the panel labeled as Fig. 4G is correctly referenced.
- In Fig 6D, perform a one-way ANOVA to determine whether the difference between the Genta and CC+Genta groups is statistically significant.
- The scale bar in Fig 6F is barely visible. Please enlarge it for clarity.
- In line 411, correct the typo “8:0 mg/L.”

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response: We agree with the reviewer’s suggestion. In addition, journal’s 150 words policy, we restrucuted the abstract in the revised manuscript, and we have made a concerted effort to clearly separate the main findings from the mechanistic interpretation. For example, in the Abstract, which was re-arranged to conform with the referee’s concern, we now state that, “Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a leading cause of bacterial infections, but treatment options are limited due to MRSA multi- drug resistance. The anti-hypertensive drug Candesartan cilexetil (CC) exhibits potent anti-MRSA activity. It permeabilizes the membrane of MRSA cells and potentiates the activity of aminoglycoside antibiotics. Here we used a variety of methods to elucidate the mechanism by which CC disrupts membrane homeostasis. We show that CC binds to bilayer lipid molecules, decreases membrane fluidity, down- regulates cell membrane and cell wall related genes and related metabolites, and decreases C20 fatty acids (C20:0). Decreasing C20:0 fatty acids confers CC- resistance, which can be reversed by C20:0 supplementation. Structural activity relationship analysis shows that the tetrazole ring and ester carbonic acid of CC are critical for antibacterial activity. Finally, CC reduces MRSA-MW2 replication in a murine MRSA abscess model, supporting a potential role of CC as a lead antimicrobial compound/potentiator against MRSA.”. Page 2, Lines 22-33. We believe this revision improves clarity and directly addresses the reviewer’s concern.
2. Supplement the direct correlation between the membrane structure of MRSA and its drug resistance. In particular, the impact of membrane lipid composition (such as phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin) on drug penetration should be emphasized to strengthen the logicality of the research background.
Response: As recommended, we have added to the Introduction to more explicitly discuss what is known about the correlation between MRSA membrane structure and drug resistance. Specifically, we added sentences emphasizing how alterations in membrane lipid composition, including phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin, impact drug penetration and contribute to resistance. This addition strengthens the rationale for investigating the membrane-targeting activity of CC. The revised Introduction now reads, “In MRSA, alterations in membrane lipid composition, particularly reduced phosphatidylglycerol or altered cardiolipin distribution, have been associated with decreased drug penetration and increased tolerance to membrane- active antibiotics. These adaptive changes stabilize the bilayer and create a barrier to antibiotic entry, thereby contributing directly to drug resistance1-3. Thus, targeting lipid composition and fluidity may represent an effective strategy to overcome intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms in MRSA. Pages 3-4, Lines 53-69.
3. Elaborate on the contrast between "CC-induced membrane rigidity" and "traditional membrane-active agents increasing fluidity", and put forward a reasonable explanation based on the membrane lipid phase transition theory.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We now added text clarifying the contrast between CC and other membrane-active agents in the context of lipid phase behavior. The revised phrase reads, “This apparent contradiction can be explained by membrane lipid phase transition theory[54]: CC selectively interacts with long-chain saturated fatty acids (C20:0) and other lipids, promoting tighter packing of lipid tails and stabilizing the gel-like phase. This rigidity compromises membrane integrity, dissipates the proton motive force, and increases permeability, resulting in bacterial killing 4, 7, 8. Page 23, Lines 498-502.
4. Discuss potential compensatory mechanisms for the absence of C20:0 synthesis-related genes in resistant mutants. For example, the substitution of other fatty acids or adaptive changes in membrane proteins.
Response: We acknowledge that none of the CC-resistant MRSA-MW2 mutants that we studied carried mutations in C20:0 biosynthesis genes, despite the importance of these lipids for CC susceptibility. A potential compensatory mechanism may involve the substitution of C20:0 fatty acids with other long-chain saturated or unsaturated fatty acids, which could maintain overall membrane integrity while reducing CC binding. Additionally, adaptive remodeling of membrane-associated proteins, such as transporters, efflux pumps, or enzymes involved in lipid modification, may further stabilize the membrane or modulate drug permeability. Such lipid and protein adaptations could collectively allow MRSA to tolerate CC without direct disruption of C20:0 biosynthesis pathways.
The revised text reads, “Although CC-resistant MRSA-MW2 mutants lacked mutations in C20:0 biosynthesis genes, resistance may arise through compensatory mechanisms, such as substituting other long-chain fatty acids for C20:0 or remodeling membrane-associated proteins, maintaining membrane integrity while reducing CC susceptibility9. Future lipidomic and proteomic studies are needed to confirm these conjectures. Discussion, Page- 24, Lines 534-537.
5. Emphasize integrated analysis of multi-omics data. For example, instead of merely listing data, explore the correlation between the down-regulation of cell wall synthesis genes in the transcriptome and the reduction of phospholipids in the lipidome.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We have now added integrated the multi-omics analysis to highlight correlations between transcriptomic and lipidomic changes. Specifically, downregulation of cell wall synthesis genes in the transcriptome correlates with decreased levels of key phospholipids (e.g., phosphatidylglycerol and phosphatidylethanolamine) in the lipidome, suggesting that CC-mediated perturbation of lipid homeostasis is linked to transcriptional regulation of membrane biosynthesis pathways. This integrated view underscores how CC disrupts both membrane composition and biosynthetic processes, contributing to its bactericidal activity.
The revised text now reads, “Integrated analysis of multi-omics data revealed that downregulation of cell wall synthesis genes in the transcriptome correlates with decreased levels of key phospholipids in the lipidome, indicating that CC disrupts membrane composition while simultaneously affecting biosynthetic pathways”. Page 21, Lines 450-453. And, “Consistent with the multi-omics findings, the coordinated downregulation of cell wall synthesis genes and the reduction in membrane phospholipids suggest that CC perturbs both structural and biosynthetic components of the S. aureus membrane, highlighting a synergistic disruption of membrane integrity”. Page 21, Lines 458-461.
6. Validation of membrane disruption mechanisms:
a. Molecular Dynamics Simulation: It is recommended to add simulations with different membrane lipid ratios (such as DOPC/DOPG/CL mixed membranes) to better approximate the real MRSA membrane environment.
The 70:30 DOPC/DOPG membrane model employed in the original submitted manuscript is a well-regarded model that has been successfully utilized in multiple high-profile computational and experimental studies.1,2 Nevertheless, the reviewer is correct that validation against additional advanced Gram-positive membrane models would be beneficial. To that end, we performed new simulations exploring the interaction between CC and a “more advanced membrane model” that was previously used to study the antibacterial action of lugdunin in a 2024 Nature Communications article by Ruppelt et al.3,4 To our knowledge, this latter model of a Gram-Positive lipid bilayer is the highest-fidelity available for simulations and contains the 9 most common lipids present in the Gram-Positive model organism Bacillus subtilis, with ratios determined by GC-MS, LC/LC-MS and MALDI-TOF findings. Key structural differences between the Ruppelt et al model and the 70:30 DOPC/DOPG include iso- and anteiso-branched lipid tails and cardiolipin (CL) molecules. In summary, new triplicate MD runs between this advanced membrane model and CC revealed no significant differences in penetration behavior or thermodynamics compared to our original 70:30 model. Unsteered MD simulations confirmed that CC readily penetrates the bilayer membrane (Figure S1while steered MD and PMF analyses (Figure S2) confirmed that this penetration is thermodynamically favored, with a ΔG of around -10 kcal mol-1 pen (compared to -8 kcal mol-1 for the 70:30 DOPC/DOPG simulations). The penetration of CC within this new membrane was slightly shallower ~17-22 Å from the bilayer center (compared to the original penetration depth of ~12-19 Å) but this is thought to be due to an increased variance in simulation box sizes with the Ruppelt et al. membrane model. Due to the parallelized nature of umbrella sampling, this variance cannot be normalized. Our simulations did note the new model yielded some buckling of the membrane plane arising from barostat limitations in the MD software AMBER24. This is likely why we have not found any literature examples of CL-containing membranes simulated using AMBER24, but instead utilizing 70:30 DOPC/DOPG. Overall, the 70:30 DOPC/DOPG model yielded comparable trends to the more advanced model and, more importantly, both models provided support for the proposed penetration of CC reported in the experimental data sections of this manuscript.
We decided to NOT include the data with the Ruppelt et al. CL-containing membranes because the paper is already very long and complicated, but these data could be included if necessary.

c. Functional Verification of Mutant Strains: Gene knockout or complementation experiments are required to confirm the contribution of mutant genes (e.g., tarS) to CC resistance, excluding the interference of other SNPs.
Response: We agree with the reviewer’s comment regarding the need to functionally verify the role of cell wall/membrane–associated genes in mediating CC susceptibility. However, we did not attempt to directly complement the tarS mutant derived from the passaging experiment because comprehensive genetic analysis is not the focus of this manuscript. Nevertheless, to partially address the referee’s concerns, we performed MIC determinations using wild-type, knockout, and complemented tarO strains (a gift from Dr. Suzzane Walker lab). tarO, like tarS, is involved in the biosynthesis of cell wall teichoic acid. Unexpectedly, however, deletion of tarO resulted in a 2-fold reduction in CC MIC (from 8 mg/L in RN4220 to 4 mg/L in ΔtarO). Restoration of tarO expression from a plasmid complemented strain reverted the MIC back to 8 mg/L, validating the specificity of the phenotype. These results definitively link cell wall architecture to CC activity and validate the functional importance of these genes in modulating susceptibility.
Based on the observation that deletion of tarO increased rather than decreased susceptibility to CC, we now added the following text in the Results section: “One particular CC-resistant mutant clone carrying mutations in purR, folC, farR, and tarS (strain MRSA-MW2-S50 from day 50 of serial passage (Supplementary Tables 6)) was chosen for further analysis (as described in the section below on structure-activity relationship studies). Interestingly, however, MRSA-MW2-S50 did not exhibit decreased levels of C20:0 lipids (Extended Data 4G), suggesting that a variety of mechanisms could lead to CC-resistance. In this regard, the observation that the CC-resistant strain MRSA-MW2-S50 contained a mutation in the tarS gene, which is required for cell-wall teichoic acid biosynthesis, prompted us to test whether a well-studied S. arueus tarO mutant exhibits CC resistance. Specifically, we tested a previously constructed deletion of the tarO gene, an isogenic derivative of the tarO mutant carrying wild-type tarO expressed on plasmid pTP63, and S. aureus strain Newman, the parent of the tarO mutants. As shown in Extended data 4H, the MICs of the Newman strain, the tarO mutant, and the complemented mutants were unexpectedly 8 mg/L, 4 mg/L and 8 mg/L, respectively. That is, the tarO mutant was more susceptible to CC than the parent strain, in contrast to our expectation. Since the ΔtarO mutant was more sensitive to CC, it is unlikely that TarO or TarS are direct molecular targets of the compound. Instead, these results indicate that TarO–TarS–dependent pathways preserve cell wall architecture and mitigate CC-induced stress. Mutations in tarS may alter WTA composition or surface charge, potentially reducing CC binding or penetration. Collectively, these findings suggest that CC activity is modulated by the integrity and glycosylation status of wall teichoic acids.” Page 15-16, Lines 316-344. The data is now included in Extended data-4H panel.
