We would like to clarify that Figures 4A, 4B, and 4C represent biologically distinct experimental conditions.
Figure 4A shows MRSA-MW2 cells with standard growth conditions treated with CC.
Figure 4B, N shows MRSA-MW2 cells grown in the presence of stearic acid and treated with CC.
Figure 4C, O shows MRSA-MW2 cells grown in the presence of oleic acid and treated with CC.
Because the cells in Figures 4B and 4C have altered membrane lipid compositions compared with standard MRSA-MW2, direct statistical comparisons between Figure 4A vs. 4B or 4A vs. 4C are not appropriate, as these represent fundamentally different biological populations. Accordingly, statistical analyses were performed within each growth condition (untreated vs. CC-treated at 4xMIC or 8xMIC), using appropriate tests, as indicated in the figure legend. Differences between fatty acid conditions are described qualitatively, reflecting the trends in membrane rigidity and susceptibility to CC.
For clarification, we removed the word “comparison” between groups and the revised text now reads, “Fig. 4B shows that growth in stearic acid increased L-GP (increase in rigidity) and that this level of rigidity was modestly increased by treatment with CC. In contrast, Fig. 4C shows that growth in oleic acid increased membrane fluidity but that treatment with CC increased rigidity to about the same levels as in cells grown in the absence of long-chain fatty acids or the presence of stearic acid. Consistent with these results, we found that MRSA-MW2 cell growth in oleic acid (Fig. 4D and G) behaves like wild type cells (Fig. 4F), but MRSA-MW2 cell growth in stearic acid decreased the ability of CC to permeabilize MW2 cells to Sytox Green (Figs. 4E) and decreased the susceptibility of MRSA-MW2 to CC-mediated killing (Figs. 4G). Page-12, Lines 250-268.
7. Fluorescence-based assays, e.g., Sytox and DiSC3(5), should be OD600nm corrected to account for any changes to the bacterial inoculum density.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. We re-did the original Sytox Green and DiSC3(5) time-course assays normalizing the data to optical densities (OD 600). CC causes rapid membrane permeabilization (Sytox Green Figure 1E and 1F uptake) and rapid dissipation of membrane potential (loss of DiSC3(5) signal) at the concentrations and time points reported. We have replaced the original panels with OD corrected data (revised Fig. 1E and 1F).

8. I am not sure that the DiSC3(5) assay has been performed correctly. When the membrane potential is intact, this voltage-sensitive dye is self-quenched, as the authors show. Compounds capable of depolarizing the membrane cause the dye to leak out, causing an increase in fluorescence. CCCP is also incompatible with this assay due to its interference with the fluorescence of DiSC3(5). Valinomycin or gramicidin would be a more suitable control, see 10.3389/fcell.2016.00029
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion.
Following the recommendation, we repeated the DiSC₃(5) membrane potential assay with little modifications according to the published study (PMC4829611) suggested by the reviewe#2 and another published study in Nature Communications (PMC11364768). Under optimized conditions using HEPES buffer supplemented with KCl and glucose, and including valinomycin and gramicidin as positive controls as shown in the revised Figure (Fig. 1F), valinomycin and gramicidin induced the expected increase in fluorescence, consistent with membrane depolarization. In contrast, treatment with CC resulted in a decrease in fluorescence in a dose-dependent manner, indicating a distinct effect on membrane potential compared to canonical depolarizing agents. These results suggest that CC does not act as a simple depolarizer but rather alters membrane dynamics in a manner that reduces DiSC₃(5) fluorescence, which is consistent with our lipidomic and fatty acid analyses indicating altered membrane homeostasis. Importantly, these data further support the conclusion that CC perturbs the bacterial membrane, albeit through a mechanism distinct from pore-forming agents. We have replaced the original panel with the new data, which is also OD normalized 600 (revised 1F).
PMC4829611: Te Winkel, J. D., Gray, D. A., Seistrup, K. H., Hamoen, L. W., & Strahl, H. (2016). Analysis of antimicrobial-triggered membrane depolarization using voltage sensitive dyes. Frontiers in cell and developmental biology, 4, 29.
PMC11364768: Li, T., Ren, X., Luo, X., Wang, Z., Li, Z., Luo, X., & Cheng, F. (2024). A foundation model identifies broad-spectrum antimicrobial peptides against drug-resistant bacterial infection. Nature Communications, 15(1), 7538.
9. I would suggest to the authors to reduce some of the modelling and SAR to improve the clarity of the message. This would make for a nice follow up paper.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion regarding the modeling and SAR sections. While we understand that reducing these sections could streamline the manuscript, we would like to retain them because the SAR studies in particular provide unique mechanistic insights that distinguish our work. As you (Reviewer 2) noted above, you have concerns about the novelty of our study in light of prior reports on CC. We believe that the inclusion of the SAR analyses, combined with the multi-omics and detailed membrane-targeting mechanistic studies, adds substantial new information that goes beyond previous reports. Specifically, the SAR studies reveal structural determinants of CC’s antibacterial activity, demonstrate its interaction with membrane lipids, and identify analogs that retain or lose activity, findings that are not reported elsewhere. We therefore feel that these sections are essential to convey the novelty and significance of our work, while also providing a strong foundation for future follow-up studies.
10. It’s not clear why Polymyxin was assayed here, since it’s not used to treat infections caused by S. aureus. Some rationale for this should be provided. Daptomycin would be a much more appropriate choice.
Response: (also refer to our response to your (referee 2) concern number 3 above). We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We agree that polymyxins are not clinically used against S. aureus. However, we included polymyxin B in our assays for two reasons: (i) polymyxin is a well-characterized cationic, membrane-active antibiotic frequently employed as a model compound to probe bacterial membrane perturbations, and thus served as a useful comparative control to validate CC’s membrane-targeting effects; and (ii) our broader research program is focused on drug repurposing strategies against Gram-negative pathogens, where polymyxins are clinically relevant. For these reasons, we assessed the interaction between CC and polymyxin B to establish potential cross-pathogen therapeutic implications. We agree with the reviewer that daptomycin is the clinically relevant lipopeptide for S. aureus, and in line with the suggestion, we have now performed combination assays of CC with daptomycin. The results show that CC is not a significant potentiator for the activity of daptomycin.
11. Since CC is only active against S. aureus in the pro-drug form, which is converted in gastric epithelial cells, how viable is this as a therapeutic? Are the MIC concentrations reported here achievable in vivo?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important question regarding the translational potential of CC. While it is correct that CC is a prodrug, our in vivo studies demonstrate that therapeutically relevant concentrations can be achieved and are effective against MRSA. Specifically, CC exhibited dose-dependent antibacterial activity in vertebrate models. Pharmacokinetic analysis in mice showed a maximum serum concentration of 8 mM CC at 12 hours post-administration, which is well above the MIC values observed in vitro. Importantly, no gross toxicity was observed based on liver and kidney profiling and histological examination. In a murine thigh infection model, 50 mg/kg CC alone reduced bacterial burden by 1-log10-CFU, gentamicin (30 mg/kg) by 2-log10-CFU, and their combination by 2.5–3.0-log10-CFU. Luminescence imaging corroborated bacterial reduction at the infection site. These results indicate that the MIC concentrations reported in vitro are achievable in vivo and that CC, alone or in combination with conventional antibiotics, has potential as a therapeutic agent. This point is now explicitly stated in the Discussion of the revised manuscript. The revised text is now added; “CC is a prodrug and our in vivo data demonstrate that therapeutically relevant concentrations are achievable and effective against MRSA-MW2. Pharmacokinetic profiling in mice showed serum levels relevant to the in vitro combinatorial MIC with clinical agents, and CC treatment significantly reduced bacterial burden in a mouse thigh infection model. These findings support the translational potential of CC as a viable antibacterial or antibiotic-potentiating agent despite its prodrug nature”. Page -24, Lines 529-537.
Minor points
1. Line 38: I don’t understand why ‘The severity of S. aureus infections is reflected in the wide variety of S. aureus virulence factors’. Some pathogens cause disease via a single toxin. I would understand if range of virulence factors was linked to range of different types of disease but not severity.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this observation. We agree that severity may not be directly proportional to the number of virulence factors. We have revised the sentence for clarity to emphasize that the diverse range of S. aureus virulence factors contributes to the spectrum of clinical manifestations and infection types, which in combination with persistence and tolerance mechanisms, complicates treatment. This revision clarifies the intended meaning and avoids implying a direct correlation between virulence factor number and severity.
The revised sentence now reads: "The broad repertoire of S. aureus virulence factors contributes to the wide spectrum of clinical manifestations and infection types, while persistence and tolerance mechanisms allow the pathogen to survive or continue limited growth in the presence of antibiotics, complicating treatment." Page 3, Lines 36-39.
2. Line39: persistence and tolerance don’t enable resistance. The former confer survival, and the latter the ability to grow, in the presence of antibiotics.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important clarification. We agree that persistence and tolerance are distinct from resistance: persistence allows a subpopulation of bacteria to survive antibiotic exposure without growing, whereas tolerance allows growth at reduced rates in the presence of antibiotics. To reflect this distinction, we have revised the relevant text in the introduction. The revised sentence now reads, “The broad repertoire of S. aureus virulence factors contributes to the wide spectrum of clinical manifestations and infection types, while persistence and tolerance mechanisms allow the pathogen to survive or continue limited growth in the presence of antibiotics, complicating treatment”. Page 3, Lines 36-39.
3. Line 52: Omit ‘lipopolysaccharides’, as S. aureus does not have LPS and LPS is not a negatively charged phospholipid.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out and we now removed “lipopolysaccharides” from the text and revised the sentence to refer only to relevant negatively charged membrane components, such as phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin
4. Line 75: Authors describe a ‘6-log10-CFU/ml’ reduction to the limit of detection. Figure 1B shows a decrease in viability from 107 – 102 CFU/ml, giving a 5-log reduction.
Response: We thank the reviewer for noting this discrepancy. The text has been corrected to accurately reflect the data shown in Figure 1B.
5. Line 79: A ~30% reduction in biofilm production, I do not believe, constitutes inhibition of biofilm production. Similarly, I do not think you can categorise CC as having biofilm eradication activity. I would recommend using tetracycline or chloramphenicol as a control for biofilm inhibition
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion, and we re-did the assay using Alamar Blue fluorescence assay to monitor the metabolically active cells and revised the text to more accurately reflect the observed effects of CC on MRSA biofilms. CC caused a modest reduction in biofilm eradication, and we agree that the term “inhibition” may overstate the effect at these concentrations. To address the reviewer’s recommendation, tetracycline was included as a control in both biofilm formation and eradication assays, demonstrating that CC’s effects are comparable or slightly less pronounced than those of a standard biofilm-active antibiotic (Fig. 1D).
We have therefore revised the text to state:" Biofilm studies show that CC treatment resulted in a dose-dependent reduction in biofilm formation and a decrease in metabolically active cells within mature biofilms, as assessed by Alamar Blue fluorescence (Fig. 1D). (Fig. 1D). We found that CC inhibited bacterial biofilm formation at concentrations as low as 0.5xMIC (4 mg/L) (Fig. 1D-right) and disrupted mature biofilms at concentrations as low as 2xMIC (16 mg/L, Fig. 1D-left) as demonstrated by using Alamar Blue to monitor the levels of metabolically active cells. While the reduction at sub-MIC concentrations was modest, these results indicate that CC can affect biofilm metabolic activity” Page 5-6, Line 94- 100.
Additionally, gene expression analyses of key biofilm-associated genes (agrA, sarA, icaA, yycG, fnbA/B) confirmed that CC modulates pathways related to biofilm formation Figure S7A-B. Functional relevance of these effects was further supported by pre-treatment experiments in Galleria mellonella, where CC pre-exposure decreased virulence of MRSA-MW2, resulting in a prolonged survival of CC-pretreated MRSA-MW2 injected larvae relative to CC-untreated controls (Figure S7C).
Taken together, these results support that CC can impair biofilm formation and reduce biofilm-associated bacterial activity, but we have removed language implying biofilm eradication.
6. Line 102: Can the authors comment on why the all-atom MD simulations performed at Vanderbilt are not in agreement with the prior simulations in reference to membrane perturbation?
Response: The apparent differences likely arise from variations in the simulation design and lipid composition used in the two studies. As a result, the Vanderbilt simulations suggest that CC interacts more dynamically with anionic lipid domains rather than uniformly disrupting the bilayer, which may explain the discrepancy. We also note that simulation timescales and force fields can contribute to different outcomes in terms of membrane perturbation. Taken together, these differences highlight how the specific membrane composition and model parameters can influence the predicted molecular interactions of CC and underscore the importance of integrating both computational and experimental data for mechanistic interpretation.

9. Line 105: A concentration of 10x MIC is used for AFM studies. Can the authors provide a justification for such a high concentration? Is this concentration clinically achievable?
Response: We used 10×MIC for AFM because high local drug exposure was required to produce rapid, reproducible membrane topography changes that are detectable by AFM within the practical time window of the experiment. AFM in this study was a mechanistic, imaging-oriented assay rather than a direct test of clinical dosing. AFM detects nanoscale topographical and mechanical changes on single cells. To visualize rapid membrane deformation, blebbing, and leakage within the timescale of a single experiment (minutes–hours) we used a supratherapeutic concentration (10×MIC). Lower concentrations produce more subtle, slower changes that are often below AFM signal-to-noise or require extended imaging periods that can introduce artefacts (tip drift, cell drying, biological heterogeneity).
10. Line 120: A sub-lethal concentration of CC is used. The authors note in line 116 that they aimed to identify the MOA by which CC kills and identify potential targets, therefore this should be repeated with a lethal concentration of CC.
Response: We intentionally used a sub-lethal concentration (4 mg/L, 0.5×MIC depending on assay) for the comprehensive transcriptomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses in order to capture primary cellular responses and pathway perturbations that precede irreversible cell death. Lethal concentrations induce rapid loss of viability and widespread secondary degradation, which can obscure upstream events and make it difficult to distinguish primary targets from downstream collapse. For this reason, sub-lethal dosing is a standard strategy when the objective is to identify early mechanistic changes rather than the end-stage consequences of cell lysis. We also emphasize that we have directly characterized CC’s lethal effects using complementary assays performed at bactericidal concentrations (≥2×MIC–10×MIC), including time-kill kinetics (Fig. 1B–C), membrane permeability and depolarization assays (Sytox Green, DiSC3(5), Fig. 1E–G), SEM/AFM/TEM/cryo-CT imaging of membrane damage (Fig. 1I–L and 1J AFM at 10×MIC), and functional killing of persisters and biofilms (Fig. 1B–D). These lethal-concentration data provide direct, orthogonal evidence of membrane disruption and rapid bactericidal activity consistent with the pathways highlighted by the sub-lethal multi-omics experiments (e.g., downregulation of fatty acid and cell-wall biosynthesis and depletion of key PG/PE species). In other words, the sub-lethal omics reveal the early pathway perturbations while the lethal-concentration assays confirm the ultimate phenotype (membrane damage and rapid killing).

34. Line 271: Could the authors comment on the improved potency at low pH despite not having membrane permeabilisation activity.
Response: Indeed, our data show that CC exhibits its highest potency at pH 4 (MIC = 2 µg/mL) even though membrane permeabilization was not detected under these conditions. We hypothesize that this improved activity at low pH may be related to changes in CC’s protonation state, which can alter its solubility, charge distribution, and ability to interact with intracellular targets. Previous studies have shown that pH can influence antibiotic activity by modulating drug uptake, ionization, and intracellular distribution (Damper & Epstein, 1981; Taber et al., 1987; Lebeaux et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2019). At pH 4, protonation of CC may enhance its diffusion across the bacterial cell wall or facilitate stronger interactions with intracellular macromolecules, leading to increased antibacterial potency even in the absence of direct membrane permeabilization. To clarify this point, we have now added text in the Results and Discussion highlighting that CC may exert antibacterial effects through both membrane-dependent and membrane-independent mechanisms, with the latter being more dominant at acidic pH. As suggested by the reviewer, we added the following text in the Results, “Interestingly, despite the absence of detectable membrane permeabilization at pH 4, CC displayed its highest potency (MIC = 2 µg/mL) under these acidic conditions. This suggests that CC may exert antibacterial effects through membrane-independent mechanisms at low pH”, Page 15, Lines 310-314.

36. Line 293- Line 295: The authors should investigate the individual involvement of these genes in CC resistance using mutants.
Response: We agree that assessing the contribution of individual genes to CC resistance using targeted mutants would be the most direct approach. Within our current resources, we performed preliminary MIC testing with a purR mutant from the NTML library, which showed increased susceptibility to CC, consistent with a role for purine metabolism in resistance. We also conducted MIC testing of multiple resistant clones obtained from mutation frequency experiments, which demonstrated a stepwise increase in CC MICs over time. Interestingly, as CC resistance increased, we observed a concurrent reduction in oxacillin MIC (from >32 mg/L at Day 1 to 8 mg/L by Day 50), suggesting a potential trade-off between CC resistance and β-lactam resistance. This pattern indicates that the adaptive mechanisms conferring CC resistance may come at the cost of altered cell wall physiology, reducing resistance to β-lactams. Such collateral sensitivity phenomena have been described in antibiotic resistance evolution and warrant deeper genetic and mechanistic investigation.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
This study found the effectiveness of candesartan cilexetil as an antibiotic against MRSA. In particular, the authors propose that the change in C20:0 fatty acids is associated with the susceptibility of bacteria to CC. While the manuscript presents intriguing data on the potential application of CC as an antibiotic using a variety of experimental approaches, it appears to lack sufficient elucidation of the underlying mechanism and its practical applicability. Moreover, the absence of detailed descriptions for the multi-omics methodology, the low quality of several figures (e.g., small text, missing scale bars), and inaccurate figure legends collectively reduce the overall clarity and credibility of the manuscript.
Major concerns
1. The authors should conduct more reliable experiments to identify the potential specific lipid target of CC. The authors should determine the mechanism by which CC treatment reduces the production of C20:0 fatty acids. Additionally, they should analyze whether the susceptibility of MRSA to CC changes when genes involved in the relevant biosynthetic pathway are knocked out or overexpressed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these suggestions. We agree that identifying the precise lipid target of CC and elucidating the genetic mechanism underlying the reduction of C20:0 fatty acids would provide deeper mechanistic insights; however, these analyses are beyond the scope of the current study. Our preliminary serial passage experiments did not yield mutants with altered C20:0 fatty acid profiles as predicted. Instead, we conducted physiological assays that modulated C20:0 levels and then demonstrated that supplementation with exogenous C20:0 fatty acids restored susceptibility to CC. These findings support the functional link between C20:0 fatty acids and CC activity.
We plan to pursue detailed lipidomics and genetic studies in future work
We now included this revised text in the Results, “One particular CC-resistant mutant clone carrying mutations in purR, folC, farR, and tarS (strain MRSA-MW2-S50 from day 50 of serial passage (Supplementary Tables 6)) was chosen for further analysis (as described in the section below on structure-activity relationship studies). Interestingly, however, MRSA-MW2-S50 did not exhibit decreased levels of C20:0 lipids (Extended Data 4G), suggesting that a variety of mechanisms could lead to CC-resistance. In this regard, the observation that the CC-resistant strain MRSA-MW2-S50 contained a mutation in the tarS gene, which is required for cell-wall teichoic acid biosynthesis, prompted us to test whether a well-studied S. arueus tar mutant exhibits CC resistance. Specifically, we tested a previously constructed deletion of the tarO gene, an isogenic derivative of the tarO mutant carrying wild-type tarO expressed on plasmid pTP63, and S. aureus strain Newman, the parent of the tarO mutants. As shown in Extended data 4H, the MICs of the Newman strain, the tarO mutant, and the complemented mutants were unexpectedly 8 mg/L, 4 mg/L and 8 mg/L, respectively. That is, the tarO mutant was more susceptible to CC than the parent strain, in contrast to our expectation. Since the ΔtarO mutant was more sensitive to CC, it is unlikely that TarO or TarS are direct molecular targets of the compound. Instead, these results indicate that TarO–TarS–dependent pathways preserve cell wall architecture and mitigate CC-induced stress. Mutations in tarS may alter WTA composition or surface charge, potentially reducing CC binding or penetration. Collectively, these findings suggest that CC activity is modulated by the integrity and glycosylation status of wall teichoic acids.”. Page 15-16, Lines 325-344.
We also utilized a strain from Nebraska Transposon Mutant Library collection and data is included. Please refer to the response for Reviewer #2, minor comment #36.
2. The precise target lipid associated with the antibacterial activity of CC should be identified (e.g., C20:0-containing phosphatidylcholine).
Response: We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the need to identify the precise lipid targets of CC. We agree with the reviewer that identifying the lipid species associated with CC activity is critical. In our study, comprehensive lipidomic profiling revealed broad remodeling of S. aureus membrane lipids, including significant decreases in multiple phospholipids such as phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), indicating general disruption of membrane integrity. In parallel, functional GC–MS analysis specifically demonstrated a marked decrease in C20:0 fatty acids in MRSA-MW2 membranes upon CC treatment and in cerulenin-treated cells, and supplementation with C20:0 lipids partially restored CC susceptibility. These results together indicate that C20:0-containing lipids play a critical role in CC-mediated membrane disruption. While the exact individual phospholipid species (e.g., phosphatidylcholine, PG, cardiolipin containing C20:0) have not yet been assigned, our data strongly support their involvement. Moreover, our, TEM analysis showed that C20:0 supplementation partially restored cell morphology in CC-treated MRSA cells, we included the revised TEM figure in Fig 2H, providing structural evidence that this lipid contributes to membrane integrity and CC-mediated disruption. While our study demonstrates that C20:0-containing membrane components are important for CC susceptibility, further lipidomic analysis coupled with phospholipid-specific reconstitution assays will be required to determine the precise phospholipid class (e.g., C20:0-containing phosphatidylglycerol or cardiolipin) that acts as the direct target.
3. While previous studies have correlated increased membrane fluidity with enhanced antibiotic effects as discussed, this study suggests that increased membrane rigidity induced by C20:0 treatment is associated with the antibacterial effect of CC. Further mechanistic studies are needed to clarify this discrepancy.
While many membrane-active agents are thought to increase fluidity, there are precedents for increased rigidity or reduced membrane dynamics in the presence of permeabilizing antibiotics or antimicrobial peptides. For example, the AMP LL-37 rigidifies the cytoplasm of E. coli (Zhu, Mohapatra & Weisshaar, 2019) ; daptomycin disrupts fluid membrane microdomains and causes rearrangement of lipids, possibly increasing order in certain membrane regions (Muller et al, 2016); AMPs in model membranes can produce structural domain reorganization (edge instabilities, thinning, etc.) that is not consistent with pure fluidization but suggests increased local order or tension in the bilayer (Zorila et al, 2029)
We hypothesize that in the case of CC-mediated rigidification, rather than fluidization, CC perturbs the delicate balance of membrane homeostasis in S. aureus, impairing cell division, membrane protein function, and permeability, thereby leading to bacterial killing. Notably, supplementation with C20:0 lipids partially restores susceptibility, supporting a lipid-specific mechanism. We agree that further studies, including real-time biophysical analyses and molecular-level imaging, will be important to fully reconcile this apparent discrepancy and clarify how CC-induced membrane rigidification contributes to antibacterial efficacy

4.The interpretation of the results regarding C20:0-lipid in this manuscript is difficult for readers to follow. For example, Figures 4Q–Y suggest that the treatment of C20:0 fatty acids enhance MRSA susceptibility to CC. However, Fig 4P shows that treatment with CC, which has antibacterial activity, actually decreases C20:0 lipid levels. This apparent contradiction raises questions about whether C20:0 lipids are indeed the potential target of CC. The authors need to provide a clearer explanation of these findings in the manuscript.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. We agree that the role of C20:0 lipids in CC-mediated antibacterial activity is complex and requires careful interpretation. Our data indicate that sub-MIC of CC treatment decreases the overall cellular levels of C20:0-containing lipids (Fig. 4P), these lipids appear to be critical for CC’s activity, as shown by functional experiments: supplementation of C20:0 to cerulenin-treated or sub-MIC CC-treated cells partially restores susceptibility to CC (Figs. 4S, 4X). This suggests that CC preferentially interacts with C20:0 lipids in the membrane to exert its antibacterial effect, and that the observed decrease in C20:0 levels after CC treatment likely reflects their consumption, remodeling, or displacement during CC-induced membrane disruption. In other words, C20:0 lipids are functionally important for CC activity even though their abundance decreases following treatment. We have revised the manuscript to explicitly clarify this interpretation, emphasizing the distinction between the absolute lipid level and its functional role as a target of CC.
5. CC is known to have side effects such as low blood pressure, elevated potassium levels, and kidney damage. Using the effective dosage shown in Figure 6, these parameters should be measured. In the case of Fig 6B, the lack of statistical significance may be due to the small sample size (low n), yet it shows a trend of increase potentially induced by CC. These measurements should be analyzed with a higher n and not only at the terminal time point, but also across multiple time points.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding potential side effects of CC. We acknowledge that parameters such as blood pressure, serum potassium levels, and kidney function markers were not measured in the current study and agree that these are critical for evaluating CC’s safety profile. The trends observed in Fig. 6B, although not statistically significant due to the limited sample size, suggest potential alterations that merit further investigation. The observed efficacy at doses below the antihypertensive range suggests a potential therapeutic window, supporting the feasibility of analog optimization before full toxicodynamic profiling. Performing these measurements with a larger cohort and multiple time points represents a different and more extensive scope of work. We plan to conduct these assays in future studies alongside CC analogs in a detailed manner. Therefore, we have included this as a limitation of the current study, and future work will provide a more comprehensive assessment of safety at therapeutically relevant doses.
We have included the following text in the revised paper,
“Although our in vivo studies demonstrate the antibacterial efficacy of CC, parameters such as blood pressure, serum potassium, and kidney function were not evaluated. Assessing these with larger cohorts and multiple time points will be addressed in future work, including evaluations of CC analogs. Page- 23, Lines 534-537.
6. The methods section does not provide details on how the metabolomics and lipidomics analyses shown in Figure 2 were performed.
Response: We now included the procedure in the Methods. Page -38-39, Lines 827- 855.
Metabolomics and Lipidomics Analysis Sample Preparation: MRSA-MW2 cells were treated with CC or control (DMSO). Six biological samples were processed: control (NC-1, NC-2, NC-3) and CC-treated (CC-1, CC-2, CC-3) and submitted to the MSF Core- UTMB. Cells were extracted using a liquid-liquid extraction with MTBE/methanol/water (10:3:2.5, v/v/v). Isotopically labeled internal standards were added prior to extraction, including a commercial lipid mix (UltimateSPLASH™ ONE) for lipidomics. The aqueous phase was used for metabolomics, and the organic phase for lipidomics. The remaining protein pellet was used to quantify total protein content using a BCA assay.
LC-MS/MS Analysis: Samples were analyzed using an Acquity Premier UHPLC system (Waters) coupled to a QTRAP 6500 mass spectrometer (SCIEX). Quality control (QC) measures included pooled QC (mixture of all samples), reference standard QC (122 metabolites), and internal standard QC. Pooled QCs were injected at the beginning, middle, and end of the batch to monitor signal stability and retention time drift.
Targeted Metabolomics: Dried aqueous phases were resuspended in 80% acetonitrile and separated on a BEH Z-HILIC column (Waters). Mobile phases were: A) 15 mM ammonium bicarbonate + 2.5 µM Agilent InfinityLab deactivator additive, pH 9; B) acetonitrile/15 mM ammonium bicarbonate (90:10, v/v) + 2.5 µM additive. A total of 207 metabolites were monitored, and 121 were detected.
Targeted Lipidomics: Dried organic phases were resuspended in dichloromethane/methanol (1:1, v/v) and separated by HILIC chromatography on a Luna NH2 column (Phenomenex). Mobile phases were: A) acetonitrile/water/hexane (92:6:2, v/v/v) + 10 mM ammonium acetate, pH 9.3; B) acetonitrile/water (1:1, v/v) + 10 mM ammonium acetate, pH 9.3. Lipids were monitored using the Lipidyzer 2.0 targeted panel.
Data Analysis: Peak areas were integrated using MultiQuant v3.0.3 (SCIEX) and normalized to appropriate internal standards using a custom R script (v4.3.1).
Statistical analyses were performed in MetaboAnalyst v6.0. Data were log10-transformed and autoscaled. Partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) was performed to compare groups. Volcano plots used thresholds of fold change ≥2 and p < 0.05. Heatmaps were generated using Euclidean distance and Ward clustering.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.

Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) represents an evolutionarily conserved machinery governing proteostasis through spatiotemporal regulation of protein degradation. While spermatogenesis involves multilayered regulatory mechanisms spanning translation to dynamic post-translational modifications (PTMs), the identity of UPS-associated E3 ligases orchestrating germ cell-specific protein turnover remains elusive. Here, we identify a testis-specific E3 ubiquitin ligase complex comprising elongin B/C, Cullin-2 (CUL2), RING-box protein-1 (RBX1), and SOCS box protein ASB9, designated ECSASB9. Genetic ablation of ECSASB9 in mice via ubiquitous Asb9 knockout (KO) or spermatid-specific elongin B/C conditional KO disrupts spermiogenesis and compromises fertility. Mechanistic studies reveal that ECSASB9 engages tubulin beta 4A (TUBB4A) through substrate recognition, catalyzing K48-linked polyubiquitination at lysine 379 (K379) to promote proteasomal degradation. Notably, Tubb4a K379R knock-in (KI) mice phenocopy the spermiogenesis defects observed upon ECSASB9 deficiency. Clinically, we identify three hemizygous missense variants in X-linked ASB9 among Chinese males with idiopathic infertility. Male mice bearing orthologous ASB9 variant exhibit oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OAT) and subfertility, mirroring human phenotypes. Taken together, our findings establish ECSASB9 as an important regulator of spermatogenic proteostasis and provide mechanistic insights into UPS-mediated tissue-specific degradation, while implicating ASB9 variants in male infertility pathogenesis.

---

## Introduction

Cellular proteostasis relies on dynamic regulation of protein synthesis and degradation, governed by a conserved enzymatic cascade involving E1 ubiquitin-activating enzymes, E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes, and E3 ubiquitin ligases. This cascade initiates with ATP-dependent activation of ubiquitin (Ub) by E1, forming a thioester bond between Ub’s C-terminus and the E1 catalytic cysteine. Ub is subsequently transferred to an E2 enzyme, generating a reactive E2~Ub intermediate. E3 ligases then orchestrate substrate specificity by recruiting both the E2~Ub complex and target proteins, catalyzing Ub transfer to substrate lysine residues. K48-linked polyubiquitination marks substrates for recognition and proteolysis by the 26S proteasome.

The remarkable diversity of E3 ligases (>600 in humans) reflects their evolutionary adaptation to target a broad array of substrates. E3s are classified into three structural families: RING (really interesting new gene), HECT (homologous to E6AP carboxyl terminus), and RBR (RING-between-RING). RING-type E3s, the largest class, utilize zinc-coordinating RING or U-box domains to bind E2~Ub and facilitate Ub transfer. Among these, cullin-RING ligases (CRLs) represent modular multi-subunit complexes assembled on cullin (CUL) scaffolds, RING-box proteins, adaptors, and substrate receptors. A prototypical CRL subclass is the ECS complex (Elongin B/C–CUL–SOCS-box protein), where SOCS-box proteins serve as substrate receptors by interacting with the Elongin B/C (ELOB/C) adaptor dimer. This adaptor recruits either a CUL2-RBX1 or a CUL5-RBX2 catalytic core, completing assembly of a functional E3 ligase that directs substrate polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.

Notably, >40 SOCS-box proteins have been identified in mammals, conferring tissue-specific functionality to ECS complexes. For instance, SOCS2 modulates growth hormone signaling through dual regulatory roles, while ASB3 suppresses antiviral immunity by targeting mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) for polyubiquitination and degradation. Tissue-restricted ECS variants include ASB15 in skeletal muscle differentiation, and ASB6 in adipocyte insulin signaling via SH2B2 (SH2B adapter protein 2) degradation. These studies collectively demonstrate that ECS complex composition dictates substrate selectivity and functional specialization across tissues. However, the mechanisms governing ECS assembly heterogeneity and its tissue-specific regulatory logic remain unresolved, necessitating systematic exploration of ECS plasticity in vivo.

In somatic cells, ASB9 is predominantly known to assemble into an ECS complex with CUL5, where it targets mitochondrial proteins such as ubiquitous mitochondrial creatine kinase (uMtCK) for degradation, thereby regulating mitochondrial structure and bioenergetics. This establishes a paradigm where ASB9–CUL5 functions in metabolic regulation. However, whether ASB9 can form alternative, tissue-specific complexes with distinct catalytic cores and functions remains an open question. To address this gap and to systematically explore the heterogeneity of ECS complexes in vivo, we performed tissue-specific proteomic profiling of endogenous ECS complexes in mice, which led to the identification of a testis-specific ECS variant, termed ECSASB9, that is important for spermiogenesis and fertility in mice and humans.

---

## Results

IP-coupled proteomic profiling identifies ECSASB9
To systematically assess the heterogeneity of the endogenous ECS complex across mammalian tissues, we conducted comprehensive interactome mapping in 11 adult mouse tissues using ELOB as bait. ELOB, together with ELOC, forms a stable adaptor dimer that is central to the assembly of ECS-type E3 ligases. This ELOB/C dimer serves a dual function: it specifically recruits SOCS-box-containing substrate receptors while simultaneously binding to the cullin (CUL2 or CUL5) scaffold, thereby bridging the substrate-recognition module to the catalytic core of the ligase.

Profiling revealed tissue-specific variability in ECS complex composition. ELOB/C and CUL2 demonstrated constitutive presence across all examined tissues. In contrast, SOCS-box proteins displayed stringent spatial restriction, with NEURL2 and ASB10 exclusively detected in heart, while VHL showed intestinal specificity. Of note, testicular heterogeneity was observed, characterized by the co-enrichment of four SOCS-box proteins: ASB1, ASB3, ASB9, and TCEB3. Among these, TCEB3 exhibited broad distribution (detected in 5/11 tissues), whereas ASB1/3/9 showed strictly testis-specific enrichment. Notably, uterus uniquely harbored both CRL2- and CRL5-type ECS complexes, with CUL5 showing uterus-specific enrichment. Collectively, our multi-tissue interactome reveals considerable combinatorial diversity in the ECS complex.

In our previous studies, we found that Asb1 and Asb3 showed abundant expression during the postmeiotic spermatid elongation phase in mice. Notably, whereas Asb3-deficient mice maintained normal fertility and spermatogenesis, ASB1 formed a functional E3 ligase complex with ELOB to orchestrate the ubiquitination of sulfide-quinone oxidoreductase (SQOR), thereby modulating hydrogen sulfide (H2S) metabolic homeostasis during spermiogenesis. This mechanistic insight was corroborated by the phenotype of Asb1-KO which exhibited compromised male fertility characterized by sperm defects and significant testicular H2S depletion. However, little is known about the distribution and function of ASB9 during spermatogenesis. To this end, we first performed a cross-species conservation analysis of ASB9, which showed that it is highly conserved across diverse taxa. Notably, the structural integrity of both Ankyrin (ANK) and SOCS domains was maintained throughout evolution, strongly suggesting an evolutionarily conserved functional role for this protein. RT‒PCR identified Asb9 as testis-enriched in both mice and humans. In addition, immunostaining uncovered strict spatiotemporal distribution of ASB9 during spermatogenesis. While core ECS components ELOB/C, CUL2, and RBX1 exhibited constitutive expression across all spermatogenic steps, ASB9 first appeared at step 8 spermatids. Its signal intensified through steps 9-14, then sharply declined by step 15. Intriguingly, TCEB3, a ubiquitously identified ECS substrate receptor, displayed complementary dynamics: present from pachytene spermatocytes to step 8 spermatids but undetectable in later steps. This reciprocally phased expression pattern suggests a model where timed replacement of TCEB3 by ASB9 reprograms ECS complex substrate specificity during late spermiogenesis.

Immunofluorescence imaging of testicular single-cell suspensions revealed a skirt-like structure of ASB9 signals surrounding the elongating spermatid head, a topography reminiscent of the transient microtubule-based manchette that is crucial for sperm head shaping. Co-immunostaining with the manchette marker α-tubulin showed precise colocalization in elongating spermatids, confirming ASB9’s location in manchette. Subsequently, we performed Co-IP assays using testicular lysates to validate the IP-LC-MS/MS results. Anti-ELOB antibody precipitated the immunoprecipitates comprising ELOB/C, CUL2, RBX1, and ASB9, demonstrating constitutive assembly of an ECS complex we term ECSASB9. Together, these data suggest testis-specific ECSASB9 functions as a manchette-resident ubiquitination machinery which may be required for sperm head morphogenesis.

Impaired spermiogenesis and fertility in Asb9-KO mice
To investigate the functional significance of ECSASB9 in male fertility, we established an X-linked ubiquitous Asb9 knockout (Asb9-KO) mouse model via CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing. Sanger sequencing verified a 13-bp deletion causing frameshift mutation in hemizygous Asb9-KO males, with subsequent Western blot and immunostaining confirming complete ASB9 protein ablation in Asb9-KO testes. Asb9-KO males exhibited marked subfertility accompanied by smaller testis sizes and lower testis weights compared to wild-type (WT) mice. Epididymal sperm analysis revealed that the sperm count, motility and progressive motility were significantly reduced in Asb9-KO mice relative to WT mice. Notably, head morphology defects, including amorphous, microcephalic, or tapered configurations, as well as acrosomal abnormalities, such as irregular shaping, fragmentation or near-complete absence, were increased in Asb9-KO mice, while tail abnormalities remained statistically comparable between the two groups. Ultrastructurally, WT sperm displayed intact acrosomal caps overlying densely condensed nuclei, whereas Asb9-KO sperm exhibited malformed heads with acrosomal defects ranging from irregular and fragmented structures to near-complete absence. In contrast, the flagellar ultrastructure of Asb9-KO sperm appeared normal, exhibiting the typical “9+2” microtubule doublet arrangement characteristic of functional sperm tails. To investigate the basis of the motility defect despite normal flagellar structure, we measured intracellular ATP levels. Sperm from Asb9-KO mice exhibited a significant reduction in ATP content compared to WT controls, indicating a state of bioenergetic deficit. These collective anomalies define a classical oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OAT) phenotype, explaining the observed subfertility in Asb9-KO males.

Histomorphometric assessment of Asb9-KO and WT testes revealed comparable populations of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells between the two groups. However, morphologically compromised spermatids were evident in Asb9-KO tubules. The increased apoptotic signals in the cauda epididymis of Asb9-KO mice suggest that these deformed spermatids may undergo apoptosis. This interpretation is supported by step-resolved morphometric analysis of Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)- and peanut agglutinin (PNA)-stained spermatids, which revealed normal spermatid numbers and head shaping through step 9 in Asb9-KO mice, but a significant reduction in spermatid number and an increase in head and acrosome defects at steps 10–16 of spermiogenesis.

The manchette, a transient microtubular scaffold composed of α/β-tubulin heterodimers, assembles transiently during mouse spermiogenesis (steps 8–14), serving as the principal architect of postmeiotic nuclear shaping. Given ASB9’s manchette-specific localization, we explored whether the deficiency of ASB9 affects manchette structure across spermiogenesis. Immunofluorescence staining and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed intact manchette assembly in Asb9-KO spermatids at steps 8–9, with normally condensing nuclei and properly overlying acrosomes. However, at step 10, the microtubule bundles in Asb9-KO spermatids were thinner than in WT spermatids, which coincided with the onset of nuclear shaping defects and aberrant acrosomal development. In later steps, aberrant elongation and disorganization of the manchette in Asb9-KO spermatids were accompanied by severe malformation of the sperm head and irregular acrosomal structure. Consequently, by late spermiogenesis when the manchette disassembles, Asb9-KO spermatids failed to complete remodeling, resulting in the production of spermatozoa with misshapen heads and malformed acrosomes. All these results indicate ASB9 as an important modulator of manchette dynamics during murine spermiogenesis, with its deficiency causing OAT through microtubule-dependent nuclear shaping defects.

Given that Asb9 mRNA is detectable in several tissues, with notable expression in the kidney, we assessed whether ASB9 deficiency led to broader pathological consequences. Histopathological examination of key organs, including the brain and lung (tissues rich in motile cilia) and the kidney, revealed no overt morphological abnormalities in Asb9-KO adults compared to WT littermates.

ASB9 facilitates the K48-linked ubiquitination of TUBB4A on K379
To identify substrates of the ECSASB9 complex critical for manchette dynamics, we performed IP-LC-MS/MS on endogenous ASB9 complexes isolated from mouse testes. Comparative analysis of two biological replicates identified 97 overlapping proteins, including ASB9, ELOB/C, and tubulin beta 4A (TUBB4A)—a β-tubulin family member. Reciprocal co-IP validated endogenous interactions between ASB9 and both ELOB/C and TUBB4A in testicular lysates. Immunofluorescence confirmed colocalization of ASB9 and TUBB4A in elongating spermatids. Notably, deficiency of ASB9 increased TUBB4A protein abundance without altering its mRNA levels, implicating post-translational regulation. Consistently, TUBB4A immunoprecipitated from Asb9-KO testes exhibited reduced poly-pan and poly-K48 ubiquitination compared to WT testes, as assessed by pan-ubiquitin and K48-specific antibodies. Given the canonical role of K48 chains in proteasomal degradation, these findings suggest TUBB4A as an ECSASB9 substrate undergoing ubiquitin-dependent degradation.

To mechanistically investigate this regulation, we co-expressed Flag-ASB9 and GFP-TUBB4A in HEK-293T cells. The reciprocal interaction was confirmed by co-IP, while ASB9 overexpression dose-dependently reduced endogenous TUBB4A levels. Cycloheximide (CHX) chase assays revealed decreased TUBB4A stability upon ASB9 overexpression. Moreover, we found that MG132, a proteasome inhibitor, could efficiently restore TUBB4A protein levels even under ASB9 overexpression. In vitro ubiquitination assays revealed that testis-derived ASB9 complexes catalyzed TUBB4A polyubiquitination, a process that was also observed in HEK-293T cells. Ubiquitin mutagenesis narrowed chain specificity to K48, as neither K6/K11/K27/K29/K33/K63 variants nor K48R (Lys48 substituted with arginine) supported conjugation.

Mapping ubiquitination sites using our published ubiquitome data of mouse testis, we identified five candidate lysines (K122, K216, K252, K297, K379) on TUBB4A. Site-directed mutagenesis revealed that only K379 mutation abolished ASB9-mediated polyubiquitination. Correspondingly, TUBB4A-K379R exhibited resistance to ASB9-driven destabilization in CHX assays, pinpointing K379 as the key residue for ECSASB9-dependent proteasomal targeting.

TUBB4A mutation phenocopies the spermiogenesis defects of ASB9 deficiency
To investigate the in vivo role of TUBB4A K379 in manchette integrity, we generated Tubb4a K379R knock-in (KI) mice via CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. Genotypic validation by Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) sequencing confirmed successful introduction of the K379R mutation. As anticipated, Tubb4a-KI mice displayed reduced K48-linked and pan-polyubiquitination of TUBB4A, concomitant with increased TUBB4A protein abundance in testes, while mRNA levels remained unaltered. Although Tubb4a-KI mice developed normally, they exhibited subfertility phenotypes. Testicular appearance and weight showed no significant differences between Tubb4a-KI and WT littermates. However, epididymal sperm analyzes revealed decreased sperm count, sperm motility, and progressive motility in Tubb4a-KI mice compared to WT mice. Furthermore, sperm head and acrosome defects were markedly increased in Tubb4a-KI mice, while tail abnormalities remained comparable to those in WT controls.

Histopathological examination revealed shared spermiogenesis defects between Asb9-KO and Tubb4a-KI mice. As shown in Fig. 4l–o, the elongating spermatids in Tubb4a-KI mice exhibited apparent nuclear and acrosomal deformation, coinciding with aberrant elongation of the manchette cytoskeleton. These structural anomalies correlated temporally with disrupted manchette-mediated nuclear shaping, phenocopying the defects observed in Asb9-KO spermatids. Collectively, these findings uncover TUBB4A K379 as a critical residue governing ubiquitination-dependent regulation of microtubule dynamics during murine spermiogenesis.

ELOB/C maintain ECSASB9 complex integrity to ensure spermiogenesis
While ELOB/C are established binding partners of ASB-family proteins, their functional necessity in ECSASB9-mediated substrate recognition remained undefined. To specifically dissect the role of the late-acting ECSASB9 complex without perturbing earlier ECS functions, we designed a spermatid-targeted knockout strategy. Although ELOB/C are expressed in multiple germ cell types, another ECS substrate receptor, TCEB3, operates from pachytene spermatocytes through step 8 spermatids. Ubiquitous or earlier knockout of Elob/c would disrupt the ECS TCEB3 complex and confound interpretation of phenotypes. To isolate the function of ECSASB9 during late spermiogenesis, we generated Tnp2-Cre transgenic mice and Elob/c-floxed mice. The Tnp2-Cre driver restricts Cre recombinase activity to spermatids beginning at step 8, thereby preserving ECS TCEB3 function while enabling selective ablation of ELOB/C in post-step 8 spermatids. Crossing these strains produced spermatid-specific Elob/c conditional knockout mice (Elob/c-cKO). Immunofluorescence staining confirmed efficient depletion of ELOB and ELOC specifically in elongating spermatids of Elob-cKO and Eloc-cKO testes, respectively.

Breeding assays revealed that Elob/c-cKO males were subfertility despite normal mating behaviors. Testis size and weight remained comparable to WT littermates. However, histopathological analysis of Elob/c-cKO epididymal sperm and testes uncovered an OAT phenotype accompanied by sperm head shaping defects and manchette disorganization, phenocopying Asb9-KO and Tubb4a-KI models.

To dissect the molecular basis of these defects, we interrogated ECSASB9 complex integrity in Elob/c-cKO testes. Immunoblot analyzes revealed coordinated reductions in core components: ELOB/C, ASB9, and RBX1. Additionally, TUBB4A protein levels in Elob/c-cKO testes were significantly increased, consistent with loss of ECSASB9-mediated ubiquitination.

Together, these data reveal ELOB/C as key adaptor for ECSASB9 complex stability, with their ablation triggering aberrant TUBB4A accumulation and consequent failure of manchette-mediated nuclear remodeling during spermiogenesis.

Identification of hemizygous ASB9 variants in four infertile men
To explore a possible role for ASB9 in human male fertility, we screened whole-exome sequencing data from a cohort of 1483 individuals with oligoasthenozoospermia. We identified four infertile men with oligoasthenozoospermia harbored hemizygous X-linked ASB9 missense variants. These included c.542C>T (p.A181V) in families F1 and F3, c.275G>A (p.G92E) in F2, and c.479T>C (p.I160T) in F4. All variants were absent or exceedingly rare in public population databases (gnomAD, 1000 Genomes Project). Furthermore, we specifically examined the data from the large-scale studies involving 2875 infertile men with primary spermatogenic failure and found that none of our reported ASB9 variants were present in that cohort. These ASB9 variants were classified as deleterious by computational predictors (SIFT, PolyPhen-2, CADD). Subsequent Sanger sequencing validated these variants in probands. Notably, all mutated residues reside within the evolutionarily conserved ANK domain of ASB9, as demonstrated by cross-species alignment.

Semen analysis of affected individuals showed severe reductions in sperm count, total motility, and progressive motility. Morphological abnormalities were observed via hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and TEM, including amorphous/tapered/small heads and acrosomal defects. These results suggest that ASB9 also plays an important role in sperm head shaping in humans, and that ASB9 variants are associated with human OAT.

Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) using sperm from variant carriers yielded fertilized embryos and blastocysts in all cases. Three of four couples achieved clinical pregnancies, supporting ICSI as an efficient reproductive strategy for men harboring pathogenic ASB9 variants.

To explore the effect of these missense mutations on ASB9 expression, HEK-293T cells were transfected with Flag-tagged ASB9-WT or mutant constructs (p.A181V, p.G92E, and p.I160T). Western blotting revealed markedly reduced ASB9-G92E protein levels compared to WT, concomitant with TUBB4A accumulation. CHX chase assays revealed rapid degradation of ASB9-G92E, which was rescued by MG132-mediated proteasome inhibition. Ubiquitination assays confirmed enhanced polyubiquitination of ASB9-G92E, indicating that p.G92E destabilizes ASB9 via UPS. Notably, despite ASB9-I160T and ASB9-A181V protein levels being comparable to WT, co-IP assays revealed a marked reduction in TUBB4A binding efficiency. This diminished interaction correlated with reduced TUBB4A polyubiquitination and consequent protein accumulation, identifying I160 and A181 as key residues for ASB9-TUBB4A interactions.

Mice bearing orthologous ASB9 variant mirror human phenotypes
Given the important role of Asb9 in murine spermatogenesis was unveiled by KO studies, we further generated CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Asb9G88E (Asb9-KI) mice (orthologous to human ASB9G92E) to validate its functional significance. PCR sequencing confirmed precise targeting of the variant. Similar to our in vitro findings, Asb9-KI testes exhibited increased K48-linked and pan-polyubiquitination of ASB9 alongside markedly reduced ASB9 protein levels, despite unchanged mRNA abundance. Conversely, TUBB4A ubiquitination was diminished in Asb9-KI mice, resulting in elevated TUBB4A protein accumulation without transcriptional alteration.

Notably, while Asb9-KI males exhibited normal mating behavior and testis size, they displayed significant subfertility. Histopathological analysis of Asb9-KI mice revealed OAT phenotypes, characterized by nuclear shaping defects and disorganized manchette structures. Additionally, ICSI using sperm from Asb9-KI males resulted in normal fertilization and development to the 2-cell stage at a rate comparable to the WT control, recapitulating the successful fertilization outcome observed in human carriers. These data conclusively establish the pathogenic cascade initiated by the ASB9G92E variant across species.
